Recently, reinforcement learning in financial markets (FinRL) has emerged as a promising direction to train agents for making profitable investment decisions. However, the evaluation of most FinRL methods only focuses on profit-related measures and ignores many critical axes, which are far from satisfactory for financial practitioners to deploy these methods into real-world financial markets. Therefore, we introduce PRUDEX-Compass, which has 6 axes, i.e., Profitability, Risk-control, Universality, Diversity, rEliability, and eXplainability, with a total of 17 measures for a systematic evaluation. Specifically, i) since most existing FinRL algorithms are only designed to maximize profit with poor performance under systematic evaluation, we introduce AlphaMix+, which leverages mixture-of-experts and risk-sensitive approaches, to serve as one strong FinRL baseline that outperforms market average on all 6 axes in PRUDEX-Compass, ii) we evaluate AlphaMix+ and 7 other FinRL methods in 4 long-term real-world datasets of influential financial markets to demonstrate the usage of our PRUDEX-Compass and the superiority of AlphaMix+, iii) PRUDEX-Compass¹ together with 4 real-world datasets, standard implementation of 8 FinRL methods, a portfolio management environment and related visualization toolkits is released as public resources to facilitate the design and comparison of new FinRL methods. problem: In the field of FinTech, machine learning algorithms are now widely applied to asset allocation and investment decisions. Examples include classic models like Mean-Variance and Black-Litterman, as well as emerging deep learning models. While these models have shown certain advantages under different market conditions, each also has its limitations. For instance, the Mean-Variance model assumes asset returns follow a normal distribution, which often doesn't align with actual market conditions. The Black-Litterman model relies on subjective view inputs, introducing a degree of subjectivity. Although deep learning models can handle complex non-linear relationships, they suffer from poor interpretability. So, what are the core differences between these various models in terms of risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation? And is it possible to combine their strengths to build a more general-purpose and effective modeling framework?
final_response:
<answer>## Executive Summary

In FinTech, asset allocation has evolved from classical mean-variance and Black-Litterman models to machine learning and deep learning approaches that better handle non-linearities and dynamic markets. Classical models rely on parametric assumptions and equilibrium views, while ML methods learn patterns directly from data, often improving out-of-sample performance. However, ML models typically lack interpretability, and classical models face distributional and subjectivity issues. Combining models—such as using ML for return prediction within mean-risk frameworks or integrating ML-derived views into Black-Litterman—can mitigate these weaknesses and build more robust, general-purpose frameworks<cite id="1">Deep reinforcement learning outperforms mean-variance and other benchmarks in asset allocation</cite><cite id="3">ML methods for supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning in portfolio construction</cite><cite id="22">Neural networks integrated with Black-Litterman for optimized portfolios</cite>.

## Core Differences: Risk Measurement

Mean-variance optimization uses variance (or standard deviation) as the sole risk measure, assuming normally distributed returns and focusing on total volatility. This approach is tractable and widely used but can misalign with investor preferences that care more about downside deviations<cite id="11">Mean-variance assumes normality and quadratic utility</cite><cite id="28">Variance as portfolio risk in modern portfolio theory</cite>. In contrast, downside risk measures such as semivariance, Value at Risk (VaR), and Conditional VaR (CVaR) target losses below a target or confidence level, better reflecting investor aversion to negative deviations<cite id="27">Downside risk measures (semivariance, target shortfall) focus on deviations below a target</cite><cite id="31">Semivariance measures downside deviations; VaR/CVaR quantify potential losses</cite>. Recent work extends Black-Litterman to use stable distributions and alternative risk measures (including VaR and CVaR), showing that distributional assumptions materially affect optimal allocations<cite id="6">Black-Litterman with stable distributions and dispersion-based risk measures</cite>.

## Core Differences: Return Prediction

Mean-variance relies on historical means as expected returns, which can be unstable and prone to estimation errors<cite id="32">Historical mean estimation is error-prone and dominates optimization error</cite>. Black-Litterman augments historical priors with subjective views, improving robustness but introducing subjectivity in view inputs<cite id="33">BL balances equilibrium returns with investor views</cite>. Machine learning and deep learning models predict expected returns from high-dimensional features, often outperforming traditional time-series models when integrated into portfolio formation<cite id="16">Deep learning and random forest outperform ARIMA in return prediction for portfolio optimization</cite><cite id="20">ML-based return prediction improves portfolio performance</cite>. Reinforcement learning (RL) learns optimal allocations directly from market data without explicit return forecasts, demonstrating superior performance in backtests across equities and indices<cite id="1">Deep RL outperforms mean-variance and minimum variance in US equities</cite><cite id="3">RL methods for portfolio weighting and allocation</cite>.

## Core Differences: Asset Allocation

Mean-variance and Black-Litterman produce static or equilibrium-based weights that depend on return assumptions and views; BL’s Bayesian fusion reduces sensitivity to input means but retains subjectivity<cite id="33">BL’s Bayesian approach to views and covariances</cite>. ML and deep learning approaches often use dynamic, data-driven allocation strategies: supervised models generate weights from predicted returns, unsupervised methods cluster portfolios, and RL optimizes weights via reward maximization over state–action spaces<cite id="3">ML frameworks for supervised, unsupervised, and RL in portfolio construction</cite>. Empirical studies show RL and ML-based allocators can beat classical benchmarks, particularly in volatile regimes, though transaction costs and overfitting remain concerns<cite id="1">RL portfolios outperform benchmarks with daily rebalancing</cite><cite id="19">ML-based asset allocation outperforms classical models</cite>.

## Limitations and Trade-offs

Mean-variance’s normality assumption often misrepresents fat-tailed, skewed markets, leading to suboptimal allocations<cite id="11">MV assumes normality</cite>. Black-Litterman’s reliance on subjective views can distort results if views are noisy or biased<cite id="33">Subjective views introduce subjectivity</cite>. Deep learning excels at non-linear relationships but suffers from poor interpretability and “black-box” behavior, complicating risk governance<cite id="3">ML/RL models can be opaque</cite>. RL’s data-driven optimization can overfit or incur high turnover costs, reducing net returns<cite id="1">Transaction costs erode performance in RL</cite>.

## Combining Models: A General-Purpose Framework

Hybrid frameworks integrate strengths across models. One approach is to use ML for return prediction within mean-risk optimization: studies show random forests and deep learning can improve MV and omega optimization when embedded in portfolio formation<cite id="16">ML return prediction enhances MV and omega</cite>. Another is to replace or augment return inputs in Black-Litterman with ML-derived views, leveraging neural networks and RL to provide objective, data-driven views<cite id="23">ML/RL-based views in Black-Litterman</cite><cite id="22">Neural networks integrated with Black-Litterman</cite>. Extending Black-Litterman to use stable distributions and downside risk measures improves robustness to non-normal returns and aligns risk with investor preferences<cite id="6">Stable distributions and VaR/CVaR in BL</cite><cite id="7">Dynamic BL with VaR/CVaR and volatility models</cite>. Finally, RL can be combined with interpretable risk measures (e.g., CVaR) to build dynamic allocators that balance performance and transparency<cite id="3">RL for portfolio weighting</cite>.

## Data-Driven Evidence

Empirical comparisons demonstrate hybrid advantages. Deep RL allocators using LSTM, CNN, and RNN architectures outperformed mean-variance, minimum-variance, risk parity, and equal-weight portfolios on US equities with daily rebalancing<cite id="1">Deep RL outperforms classical benchmarks</cite>. In China’s equity market, ML-based return prediction integrated with MV and omega optimization yielded superior results, with random forest predictions consistently outperforming deep learning in preselection<cite id="16">ML prediction improves portfolio performance</cite>. Dynamic BL portfolios using DCC volatility and downside risk measures beat benchmarks in both in-sample and out-of-sample tests, with lower empirical VaR/CVaR<cite id="7">Dynamic BL with VaR/CVaR and volatility models</cite>. Broader surveys indicate ML shows promise for active portfolio management but requires caution against pitfalls like overfitting and high turnover<cite id="21">ML for active portfolio management</cite>.

## Recommendations

- Use ML for return prediction within mean-risk frameworks (e.g., MV, semivariance, omega) to reduce estimation error and improve robustness<cite id="16">ML prediction in portfolio optimization</cite><cite id="17">Semivariance as a downside risk measure</cite>.
- Integrate ML-derived views into Black-Litterman to reduce subjectivity while leveraging market insights<cite id="23">ML/RL views in BL</cite><cite id="22">Neural networks with BL</cite>.
- Adopt stable-distribution assumptions and downside risk measures in BL to better reflect market realities<cite id="6">Stable distributions and dispersion-based risk</cite><cite id="7">Dynamic BL with VaR/CVaR</cite>.
- Apply reinforcement learning for dynamic allocation while incorporating interpretable risk constraints (e.g., CVaR) and monitoring transaction costs<cite id="3">RL for portfolio weighting</cite><cite id="1">RL performance and costs</cite>.

## Conclusion

Classical models provide tractable, equilibrium-based allocations but depend on strong assumptions and subjective inputs. ML and deep learning capture complex market dynamics and improve out-of-sample performance but lack interpretability. Combining models—using ML for return prediction, ML/RL for views, and stable-distribution, downside-risk BL—can build general-purpose frameworks that are robust, interpretable, and effective across diverse market conditions<cite id="1">Deep RL advantages</cite><cite id="3">ML frameworks</cite><cite id="22">BL with neural networks</cite><cite id="6">Stable distributions and risk measures</cite>.</answer>

original_data.problem: In the field of FinTech, machine learning algorithms are now widely applied to asset allocation and investment decisions. Examples include classic models like Mean-Variance and Black-Litterman, as well as emerging deep learning models. While these models have shown certain advantages under different market conditions, each also has its limitations. For instance, the Mean-Variance model assumes asset returns follow a normal distribution, which often doesn't align with actual market conditions. The Black-Litterman model relies on subjective view inputs, introducing a degree of subjectivity. Although deep learning models can handle complex non-linear relationships, they suffer from poor interpretability. So, what are the core differences between these various models in terms of risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation? And is it possible to combine their strengths to build a more general-purpose and effective modeling framework?

problem: Summarize the global investments, key initiatives, and outputs related to Artificial Intelligence (AI) by major international consulting firms (e.g., Big Four, Accenture, MBB, IBM, Capgemini). Cover aspects such as AI-driven products/services, client case studies, application scenarios, strategic directions, and talent development programs.
final_response:
<answer>## Executive Summary

Major international consulting firms have accelerated investments and launched strategic initiatives to capture the generative AI wave, with notable commitments from the Big Four and MBB firms. The Big Four collectively invested over $4B in AI, including PwC’s $1B US investment, KPMG’s $100M in Google Cloud and $25M in Vertex AI, Deloitte’s $1.5B via Deloitte Digital, and EY’s $1.4B EY.ai and AI Institute. McKinsey and BCG reported significant revenue contributions from AI and tech advisory, with McKinsey estimating 40% of revenue from AI and tech and BCG reporting $2.7B from AI-related advisory in 2024. ## Global Investments

- PwC US announced a $1B investment over three years to expand and scale AI capabilities, building on its long-standing commitment to AI<cite id="14">PwC US makes $1 billion investment to expand and scale capabilities in AI</cite>.
- KPMG committed $100M to its Google Cloud practice, estimating $1B incremental revenue, and $25M to Vertex AI via its Vertex AI Alliance, with a joint AI center in Hyderabad<cite id="15">KPMG Invests $100M in Google Cloud Alliance to Accelerate Enterprise Adoption of AI for Clients</cite><cite id="13">KPMG global AI in finance report</cite>.
- Deloitte Digital raised $1.5B through a SPAC to scale generative AI, with the Deloitte AI Institute tracking enterprise adoption and challenges<cite id="12">State of Generative AI in the Enterprise 2024 | Deloitte US</cite><cite id="13">KPMG global AI in finance report</cite>.
- EY invested $1.4B to create EY.ai and launched the EY AI Institute, with a global AI in finance report and EU AI Hub<cite id="13">KPMG global AI in finance report</cite><cite id="18">AI strategies for 8 of the world’s top consultancies</cite>.
- McKinsey reported that 40% of its revenue comes from AI and tech advisory<cite id="16">BCG overtakes McKinsey in Headcount…Thanks to talent from India!</cite>.
- BCG generated $2.7B from AI-related advisory in 2024, with over 18,000 custom GPTs and internal tools like Deckster<cite id="17">How Big Consulting Firms Profit Massively from AI Consulting</cite><cite id="16">BCG overtakes McKinsey in Headcount…Thanks to talent from India!</cite>.
- Capgemini announced a €2B investment over three years to strengthen AI leadership and trained over 120,000 employees on generative AI<cite id="22">Capgemini announces ‘augmented engineering’ offerings powered by Gen AI</cite>.
- IBM committed $3B to scale AI for business and society, including AI for Business and apprenticeships<cite id="26">IBM invests $3 billion to scale AI for business and society</cite>.

## AI-Driven Products and Services

- Accenture launched AI Refinery, a platform to help clients build custom AI models, and integrated third-party tools like Martian’s LLM router and Cresta’s contact center AI to improve routing and productivity<cite id="9">Accenture Invests in Cresta to Improve Efficiency and Productivity in Contact Centers with Generative AI</cite><cite id="6">Accenture Invests in Martian to Bring Dynamic Routing of Large Language Queries and More Effective AI Systems to Clients</cite>.
- Accenture also co-invested in a Copilot business transformation practice with Microsoft and Avanade to securely and responsibly reinvent business functions with generative and agentic AI<cite id="7">Accenture, Microsoft and Avanade Help Enterprises Reinvent Business Functions and Industries with Generative AI and Copilot</cite>.
- KPMG’s audit workflow uses KPMG Clara, and the firm’s AI in finance report highlights digitizing data estates and leveraging AI for insights<cite id="13">KPMG global AI in finance report</cite>.
- Deloitte’s AI Institute tracks enterprise adoption and challenges, including examples like chatbots, code generation, and failure scenarios for predictive maintenance<cite id="12">State of Generative AI in Enterprise 2024</cite>.
- EY.ai and the EY AI Institute support enterprise adoption, with a global AI in finance report and EU AI Hub<cite id="18">AI strategies for 8 of the world’s top consultancies</cite>.
- McKinsey’s AI and tech advisory covers strategy, operations, and digital transformation, with a focus on AI governance and responsible use<cite id="16">BCG overtakes McKinsey in Headcount…Thanks to talent from India!</cite>.
- BCG offers AI maturity assessments and advisory services, with a global AI maturity survey indicating many economies are underprepared for AI disruption<cite id="19">BCG、世界の国・地域別AI成熟度を调査。日本はAIの影响を受けやすい产业构造だが、対応力も高い「バランス型挑戦者」タイプ</cite>.
- Capgemini’s augmented engineering offerings include generative AI tools for engineering and R&D, with a Gen AI Campus training program and case studies in energy and manufacturing<cite id="22">Capgemini announces ‘augmented engineering’ offerings powered by Gen AI</cite><cite id="21">Fuelling the Future of Energy</cite>.
- IBM’s AI for Business provides AI consulting, integration, and training, with apprenticeships to develop AI skills<cite id="26">IBM invests $3 billion to scale AI for business and society</cite>.

## Client Case Studies and Application Scenarios

- Capgemini implemented Microsoft’s Digital Contact Centre and Copilot in Dynamics 365 for an energy client, achieving increased customer and employee satisfaction, a 50% reduction in average wrap-up time, and a 51% efficiency gain in refinery logistics through data integration<cite id="21">Fuelling the Future of Energy</cite>.
- Accenture’s integration of Martian’s LLM router into AI Refinery enables dynamic routing of large language queries to optimize cost and performance<cite id="6">Accenture Invests in Martian to Bring Dynamic Routing of Large Language Queries and More Effective AI Systems to Clients</cite>.
- Accenture’s generative AI in contact centers with Cresta’s AI software is projected to yield 25% higher revenue after five years for companies applying it to customer-related initiatives<cite id="9">Accenture Invests in Cresta to Improve Efficiency and Productivity in Contact Centers with Generative AI</cite>.
- Deloitte’s survey highlights adoption across functions and examples such as chatbots, code generation, and predictive maintenance failure scenarios<cite id="12">State of Generative AI in Enterprise 2024</cite>.
- KPMG’s audit workflow leverages Clara to integrate AI into finance and audit processes<cite id="13">KPMG global AI in finance report</cite>.

## Strategic Directions

- The Big Four are scaling AI via co-investments, accelerators, and alliances, with Deloitte’s SPAC and KPMG’s Google Cloud and Vertex AI commitments<cite id="12">State of Generative AI in Enterprise 2024</cite><cite id="15">KPMG Invests $100M in Google Cloud Alliance to Accelerate Enterprise Adoption of AI for Clients</cite><cite id="13">KPMG global AI in finance report</cite>.
- McKinsey and BCG are emphasizing AI governance, responsible use, and AI maturity assessments, with McKinsey’s AI advisory contributing 40% of revenue<cite id="16">BCG overtakes McKinsey in Headcount…Thanks to talent from India!</cite><cite id="19">BCG、世界の国・地域別AI成熟度を调査。日本はAIの影响を受けやすい产业构造だが、対応力も高い「バランス型挑戦者」タイプ</cite>.
- Capgemini is investing €2B over three years and training 120,000 employees on generative AI to strengthen AI leadership and deliver augmented engineering services<cite id="22">Capgemini announces ‘augmented engineering’ offerings powered by Gen AI</cite>.
- IBM’s $3B investment focuses on scaling AI for business and society, with AI for Business and apprenticeships to build a skilled workforce<cite id="26">IBM invests $3 billion to scale AI for business and society</cite>.
- Accenture is integrating third-party AI tools and forming a Copilot transformation practice to help clients securely and responsibly reinvent business functions<cite id="7">Accenture, Microsoft and Avanade Help Enterprises Reinvent Business Functions and Industries with Generative AI and Copilot</cite><cite id="6">Accenture Invests in Martian to Bring Dynamic Routing of Large Language Queries and More Effective AI Systems to Clients</cite>.

## Talent Development Programs

- Accenture’s AI Refinery integrates third-party AI tools and emphasizes upskilling clients and teams to build custom AI models<cite id="9">Accenture Invests in Cresta to Improve Efficiency and Productivity in Contact Centers with Generative AI</cite><cite id="6">Accenture Invests in Martian to Bring Dynamic Routing of Large Language Queries and More Effective AI Systems to Clients</cite>.
- KPMG’s AI in finance report and Clara platform underscore the integration of AI into audit and finance workflows, with co-investment in Vertex AI and a joint AI center<cite id="13">KPMG global AI in finance report</cite>.
- Capgemini’s Gen AI Campus trained over 120,000 employees on generative AI tools and established a dedicated generative AI practice to scale capabilities<cite id="22">Capgemini announces ‘augmented engineering’ offerings powered by Gen AI</cite>.
- IBM’s apprenticeships aim to develop AI skills and prepare the workforce for AI-driven business<cite id="26">IBM invests $3 billion to scale AI for business and society</cite>.
- BCG introduced ChatGPT Enterprise to its employees and created over 18,000 custom GPTs for internal tasks, demonstrating internal AI adoption and tooling<cite id="16">BCG overtakes McKinsey in Headcount…Thanks to talent from India!</cite>.

## Outlook

Analysts project the AI market for products and services to reach up to $990B by 2027, reinforcing the strategic bets by consulting firms<cite id="20">Market for AI products and services could reach up to $990 billion by 2027, finds Bain & Company’s 5th annual Global Technology Report</cite>. As firms scale AI offerings and talent programs, the emphasis on responsible AI, governance, and measurable outcomes will likely shape future client engagements and competitive differentiation<cite id="17">How Big Consulting Firms Profit Massively from AI Consulting</cite><cite id="19">BCG、世界の国・地域別AI成熟度を调査。日本はAIの影响を受けやすい产业构造だが、対応力も高い「バランス型挑戦者」タイプ</cite>.</answer>

The research is building upon the OneOffice Premier League Table and HfS' Intelligent Automation research stream. Furthermore, we have published assessments about AI buildings blocks including the emerging Watson ecosystem and the emergence of virtual agents. Expanding on those insights, we are taking stock on how service providers are progressing on blending AI into their delivery capabilities. At the same time, we are calling out the dynamics around the emerging technology vendors that are at the forefront of the paradigm shift from labor-centric to data-centric models, and notions of increasingly unattended automation. Those insights not only provide guidance on the progress toward the OneOffice, but they also provide a better sense of the scale along with timelines of service delivery transformation. Thus, we continue to broaden the discussion on automation beyond robotic process automation (RPA) and the rudimentary basics of automation to fix legacy processes and applications. The key question is not whether or not automation is a prerequisite to AI, cognitive, and other elements up the value chain, or whether or not these are mutually exclusive concepts and frameworks. Rather, we are trying to understand how AI can transform business operations and how buyers need to think about more data-centric approaches. We are moving beyond just business process-centric scenarios. As our OneOffice framework has demonstrated, for the value of "digital" to go beyond of the narrow confines of customer experience, organizations have to overcome the traditional silos. The fundamental question is: How should organizations invest in their digital underbellies and intelligent digital processes - and their talent to manage it all - to enable the true Digital OneOffice? The Digital OneOffice Framework is all about the design and implementation of the organizational digital experience and the creation of an intelligent, single office to execute and support it. In a few months, we won't be talking nearly as much about intelligent automation and digital technology as the critical "value levers" for operations, as they become an embedded part of the fabric of the future operations platform for new generation organizations. Instead, we will be talking about an integrated support operation having the digital prowess to enable its organization to meet customer demand - as and when that demand happens. Everything about the digital organization is about engaging people by responding to their needs instantaneously using their choice of medium to interact with it, whether it's by voice, chat box, text, Facebook messenger, email, or virtual agent. In this context, "Digital" describes the interactive channels that drive customer engagement such as cognitive agents, interactive tools, mobile, social, text, and chat. "OneOffice" describes the enabling technologies, such as unified analytics and cognitive automation, that enable real-time predictive capabilities and an engaging digital experience that unifies all the stakeholders across the organization: the customers, partners, and employees. problem: Is there a general method for solving a first-price sealed-bid auction with two bidders who have independent private values drawn from different distributions (i.e., ex-ante asymmetric bidders)?
final_response:
<answer>
## Executive summary

There is no single formula that applies to all cases, but there are general methods for solving first-price sealed-bid auctions with two ex-ante asymmetric bidders who have independent private values. In particular, one method is to derive the equilibrium bid function by solving an integral equation (often expressed as a differential equation) using the first-order condition for optimal bidding; boundary conditions are typically that the inverse-bid function maps the lowest possible bid to the lowest possible value and the highest possible bid to the highest possible value. Complementing this, analytic solutions are available for special cases where the bidders’ distributions are uniform on bounded intervals, and fully automated numerical algorithms are available for general distributions. In contrast, when bidders have discrete valuations, the structure of equilibria can differ in nontrivial ways from the continuous case, underscoring the need for case-specific treatments<cite id="19">the equilibrium inverse-bid functions solve [an integral equation]… subject to ϕn(0)=0 and ϕn(¯s)=¯vn</cite><cite id="13">we provide analytic solutions for any asymmetric …rst-price auction… with two buyers having valuations uniformly distributed</cite><cite id="9">a powerful, fully automated, and numerically robust algorithm to compute (inverse) equilibrium bid functions for asymmetric, Independent Private Values, First-Price auctions</cite><cite id="4">we consider an asymmetric auction setting with two bidders such that the valuation of each bidder has a binary support… we show that the equilibrium is unique and that the inverse bidding functions are not differentiable at the integer points</cite>.

## Theoretical foundation and general method

In a two-bidder first-price auction, the equilibrium strategy is typically characterized by solving the bidder’s Bayesian first-order condition for optimal bidding. Because the bidder’s bid must be increasing in her value to be an equilibrium, one can invert the bid function and derive a differential equation for the inverse-bid function that depends on the opponent’s distribution and the cumulative distribution function of the opponent’s value. In practice, this integral equation can be converted into a differential equation and solved with boundary conditions that the lowest bid corresponds to the lowest possible value and the highest bid corresponds to the highest possible value<cite id="19">the equilibrium inverse-bid functions solve this pair of differential equations, subject to ϕn(0)=0 and ϕn(¯s)=¯vn</cite>. This approach applies generally to independent private values, regardless of whether the distributions are continuous or discrete, although the form of the solution will vary depending on the specific distributions<cite id="19">the differential equations… apply to asymmetric independent private values</cite>.

## Special case: uniform distributions

When the bidders’ valuations are uniformly distributed over bounded intervals, analytic solutions for the inverse-bidding functions are available for any asymmetric case. These solutions unify previously known subcases, such as symmetric distributions and commonly known valuations, and are continuous in the support parameters and the minimum bid, which facilitates comparative statics and robustness analysis<cite id="13">analytic solutions for any asymmetric …rst-price auction… consistent with subcases… solution is continuous in the support and m</cite>. For example, in the symmetric case where both bidders face the same minimum value and the upper bounds are equal, the solution reduces to the standard symmetric first-price equilibrium<cite id="13">consistent with… Griesmer et al. (1967) when v1=v2 and Vickrey (1961) when one valuation is commonly known</cite>.

## Numerical methods for general distributions

For arbitrary distributions (including discrete ones), numerical algorithms can be used to compute the equilibrium inverse-bid functions. These algorithms solve the integral equations arising from the first-order conditions using local Taylor-series expansions and are fully automated, highly accurate, and flexible enough to handle user-specified distributions (analytical or empirical), as well as extensions to reserve prices and other statistics<cite id="9">fully automated and numerically robust algorithm… built-in algebra of local Taylor-series expansions… computes (inverse) bid functions and auxiliary statistics</cite>. This provides a practical general method when analytic solutions are not available<cite id="9">tool of unparalleled flexibility for the numerical investigation of theoretical conjectures</cite>.

## Caveats and exceptions

Even within the independent private values framework, the structure of equilibria can differ from the continuous case when valuations are discrete. In particular, inverse bidding functions may not be differentiable at certain points, which can affect the applicability of differential-equation methods and highlights the importance of verifying equilibrium conditions directly<cite id="4">inverse bidding functions are not differentiable at the integer points</cite>. More broadly, in richer auction environments where bidders receive signals about opponents’ valuations, revenue equivalence between first- and second-price auctions can break down, and efficiency properties can differ, but these go beyond the basic two-bidder first-price setting<cite id="7">revenue equivalence between the first and second price auctions breaks down… second price auction is always efficient… first price auction may be inefficient</cite>.

## Practical guidance

To solve a two-bidder first-price auction with independent private values from different distributions, follow these steps:
1. Write down the first-order condition for optimal bidding and derive the integral equation for the inverse-bid function.
2. Convert the integral equation into a differential equation and solve it with boundary conditions ϕn(0)=0 and ϕn(¯s)=¯vn.
3. If the distributions are uniform on bounded intervals, use the analytic solutions tailored to the asymmetric supports<cite id="13">analytic solutions for any asymmetric …rst-price auction… with uniform distributions</cite>.
4. If the distributions are general or discrete, implement a numerical algorithm that solves the integral equations and computes inverse-bid functions and auxiliary statistics<cite id="9">fully automated algorithm… computes (inverse) bid functions and auxiliary statistics</cite>.
5. Verify that the solution satisfies the equilibrium conditions, especially when dealing with discrete distributions where differentiability may fail<cite id="4">unique equilibrium with inverse bidding functions not differentiable at integer points</cite>.

## Conclusion

There is no universal formula that applies across all asymmetric two-bidder first-price auctions with independent private values, but there are general methods—both analytic and numerical—that can be applied depending on the form of the distributions. The integral-equation approach with boundary conditions provides a unified theoretical foundation, while uniform-distribution analytic solutions and numerical algorithms offer practical tools for computation<cite id="19">integral equation and differential equations with boundary conditions</cite><cite id="13">analytic solutions for asymmetric uniform distributions</cite><cite id="9">numerical algorithm for general distributions</cite>.
</answer>

The Effect of Bidders' Asymmetries on Expected Revenue in Auctions*
Estelle Cantillont
First draft: April 1999
This version: October 2000
Abstract
Bidders' asymmetries are widespread in auction markets. Yet, their impact on behavior and, ultimately, revenue and profits is still not well understood. In this paper, I define a natural benchmark auction environment to which to compare any private value auction with asymmetrically distributed valuations. I show that the expected revenue from the benchmark auction always dominates that from the asymmetric auction, both in the first price auction and the second price auction. These results formalize and make transparent the idea that competition is reduced by bidders' asymmetries. The paper also contributes to a better understanding of competition and the nature of rents in auction markets. Anonymity of the allocation mechanism seems to be an important factor.

Asymmetric First-Price Auctions with Uniform Distributions: Analytic Solutions to the General Case
Todd R. Kaplany and Shmuel Zamirz
December 25, 2007
Abstract
We provide analytic solutions for any asymmetric …rst-price auction, both with and without a minimum bid m , for two buyers having valuations uniformly distributed on \([\underline{v}_{1}, \bar{v}_{1}]\) and \([\underline{v}_{2}, \bar{v}_{2}]\) . We show that our solutions are consistent with the previously known subcases studied by Griesmer et al. (1967), when \(\underline{v}_{1}=\underline{v}_{2}\) ; and Vickrey (1961), when one valuation is commonly known. We also show that the solution is continuous in \(\underline{v}_{1}\) , \(\bar{v}_{1}\) 2 \(\underline{v}_{2}\) , \(\bar{v}_{2}\) and m . Several interesting examples are presented, including a class where the two bid functions are linear.
1 Introduction
While research on auctions, including asymmetric auctions, has grown significantly in recent years, there are still very few analytic solutions of …rst-price

auctions outside the symmetric case. Surprisingly, even what is possibly the most natural environment to study has not been solved analytically, namely, that with two buyers and private values drawn from independent but asymmetric uniform distributions. This is a fundamental case that would be useful to test conjectures, do comparative statics, or illustrate important features of auction design.
The uniform distribution plays a central role in Bayesian statistics (“in the veil of ignorance”) in the same manner that the normal distribution plays a central role in econometrics. Furthermore, it is a reasonable approximation if the true distributions are not far from uniform in view of the continuity result of Lebrun (2002). Perhaps, one reason it has not been solved until this
point is that the problem in general has been thought to be intractable.1
A solution does exist to a special case, dating back to Griesmer et al. (1967), with distributions \(V_{1} ~ U[0,1]\) , \(V_{2} ~ U[0, \beta]\) that has the following equilib
rium inverse-bid functions:2 
\[v_{1}(b)=\frac{2 b \beta^{2}}{\beta^{2}-b^{2}\left(1-\beta^{2}\right)}, v_{2}(b)=\frac{2 b \beta^{2}}{\beta^{2}+b^{2}\left(1-\beta^{2}\right)} . (1)\]

However, this result has the restriction that the distribution of buyers’ values have the same lower end.3 This is a substantial assumption: it restricts the asymmetry between the buyers to one dimension, namely, one distribution being a “stretch” of the other while ignoring di¤erent aspects of strength like “shifts”. For example, if the distribution of one buyer’s value is \(U[0,1]\) , then the second buyer could be considered stronger for having \(U[0,2]\) or for having distribution \(U[1 / 2,1]\) : In the …rst case (stretching), he is stronger in the sense that he may have higher values (in [1; 2]), while in the second case he is stronger in the sense that he cannot have low values (in [0; 1=2]).

problem: In ecology, how do birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration? What cues and disturbances influence this process?
final_response:
<answer>## Overview

Birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration by integrating multiple cues from their environment, including the sun, stars, polarized light, Earth’s magnetic field, and landmarks. These cues are processed by specialized sensory systems and cognitive maps, enabling birds to maintain accurate headings over long distances<cite id="2">Birds use a combination of compass and map senses, including the sun, stars, polarized light, and magnetic fields, and they rely on cognitive maps for spatial orientation</cite>. Recent synthesis emphasizes that navigation is not driven by a single mechanism but rather by a suite of systems operating in concert<cite id="6">Migratory navigation in birds is not based on a single mechanism but involves multiple navigation systems</cite>.

## Orientation Compasses: Sun, Stars, and Polarized Light

Celestial cues are fundamental to short- to medium-range orientation. Birds adjust their flight direction relative to the sun’s position using an internal circadian clock to account for time of day, a behavior known as the “sun compass”<cite id="7">The sun compass mechanism allows birds to adjust their heading based on the sun’s position and a circadian clock</cite>. Experiments in planetariums have demonstrated that many migrants can use stars and polarized skylight for orientation, with polarized light providing a reliable compass under overcast conditions<cite id="2">Experiments in planetariums show that birds use stars and polarized light for orientation</cite>. Some species can even use the position of the Milky Way and prominent constellations, with the North Star (Polaris) serving as a stable reference point<cite id="6">Birds can use the Milky Way and constellations, with Polaris as a fixed reference</cite>.

## The Magnetic Compass: A Global Reference

Birds also rely on Earth’s magnetic field for navigation, using two magnetically sensitive mechanisms: a polarity (compass) sense that detects magnetic north and an intensity (inclination) sense that detects field strength and tilt<cite id="2">Birds use both polarity and inclination magnetoreception to detect magnetic north and field strength</cite>. The magnetic compass is thought to be a “pure” compass, providing directional information without positional data, and it is particularly valuable at low latitudes where celestial cues are less reliable<cite id="2">The magnetic compass is a directional cue that is especially useful at low latitudes</cite>. Laboratory studies using Helmholtz coils have shown that birds can detect subtle changes in magnetic field parameters and adjust their headings accordingly<cite id="1">Experiments using Helmholtz coils demonstrate birds’ ability to detect and respond to magnetic field changes</cite>.

## The Map Sense: Determining Where You Are

While compasses provide direction, birds also need a map to determine their position relative to the destination. The most widely accepted map mechanism involves a light-dependent, magnetoreceptive system in the retina that detects variations in the magnetic field across space, allowing birds to infer their geographic location<cite id="2">A light-dependent magnetoreceptive system in the retina provides birds with a map sense</cite>. This system is supported by evidence that magnetite-based receptors in the upper beak may contribute to magnetic sensing, and that radical-pair reactions in cryptochromes in the eye are central to detecting directional cues<cite id="9">Birds detect magnetic signals via magnetite in the upper beak and radical-pair reactions in cryptochromes</cite>. Together, the compass and map senses enable birds to plan routes and correct headings during migration<cite id="2">Compass and map senses work together to guide migratory birds</cite>.

## Landmarks and Learned Routes

In addition to celestial and magnetic cues, birds use landmarks and learned routes for navigation, especially over shorter distances or in familiar regions<cite id="10">Birds can use visual landmarks and learned routes for navigation</cite>. Some studies suggest that olfactory cues may also play a role in homing and migration, though their contribution varies by species and context<cite id="9">Olfactory cues may be used by migrating birds alongside other signals</cite>.

## Disturbances to Navigation

Natural and anthropogenic disturbances can disrupt these cues and compromise navigation. Weather conditions such as cloud cover can obscure celestial cues, forcing birds to rely more heavily on the magnetic compass and increasing the risk of navigational errors<cite id="1">Cloud cover can reduce reliance on celestial cues and increase dependence on the magnetic compass</cite>. Magnetic field variability due to geomagnetic storms or local anomalies can also interfere with magnetic sensing, potentially causing deviations in flight paths<cite id="1">Geomagnetic disturbances can alter magnetic field characteristics and affect navigation</cite>.

Human activities pose significant threats. Artificial light at night disorients nocturnal migrants by overwhelming their light-dependent compasses, leading to collisions with illuminated buildings and other structures<cite id="14">Artificial night lighting disrupts birds’ orientation mechanisms and increases collision risk</cite>. Studies show that the amount of light emitted from buildings is a strong predictor of bird-window collisions, with steady-burning red and white lights being particularly attractive<cite id="13">Lighted window area predicts fatal collisions; steady-burning red and white lights increase risk</cite><cite id="12">Birds are attracted to or disoriented by steady-burning lights, increasing collision risk</cite>. Wind turbines and communication towers further contribute to collision mortality, especially when birds are navigating under poor visibility<cite id="11">Collisions with manmade structures, including wind turbines and towers, are a major migration hazard</cite>.

Climate change and habitat loss also impact migration by altering stopover sites and weather patterns, which can force birds to adjust routes and timing, sometimes beyond their navigational capacity<cite id="11">Climate change and habitat loss affect migration success by altering stopover habitats and weather conditions</cite>. These disturbances highlight the fragility of avian navigation systems and the need for conservation strategies that minimize anthropogenic interference<cite id="14">Conservation efforts should reduce artificial light and structural hazards to mitigate navigation failures</cite>.

## Conclusion

Birds achieve precise navigation during migration by integrating multiple compasses (sun, stars, polarized light, magnetic) with a cognitive map that provides positional information<cite id="2">Integration of compass and map senses enables precise navigation</cite>. While these systems are robust, they are sensitive to both natural variability and human-induced disturbances, which can lead to navigational errors and increased mortality<cite id="1">Natural variability in cues can challenge navigation</cite><cite id="14">Human disturbances, particularly light and structures, disrupt orientation and increase collision risk</cite>. Understanding and mitigating these threats is essential to preserving migratory connectivity and the ecological integrity of bird populations<cite id="11">Migration hazards underscore the need for conservation to protect stopover habitats and reduce anthropogenic threats</cite>.</answer>

problem: How to conduct comprehensive and accurate situational awareness of space targets in the cislunar space, and support the effectiveness of short-term cislunar space tracking and monitoring tasks?
final_response:
<answer>## Executive Summary

Cislunar space situational awareness (CSSA) requires a multi-sensor, multi-platform architecture that leverages ground-, space-, and airborne assets to detect, track, and characterize artificial objects across dynamically complex orbits. Comprehensive and accurate situational awareness is supported by visibility- and observability-aware orbit determination, data fusion across optical, radar, and X-band tracking, and adaptive sensor tasking that exploits favorable viewing geometries and lunar phases. Short-term tracking and monitoring effectiveness can be further improved by optimizing phasing, revisit rates, and constellation design, and by employing robust state estimation and association techniques for non-cooperative targets<cite id="1">constellation design and sensor-tasking formulations for CSSA</cite><cite id="11">visibility-informed covariance analysis and optimal observation windows</cite><cite id="12">parametrization and uncertainty quantification for xGEO/cislunar SDA</cite><cite id="20">adaptive sensor tasking for non-cooperative cislunar objects</cite>.

## 1. Architecture and Constellation Design

A robust CSSA architecture should integrate space-based observers in strategic orbital slots (e.g., libration point orbits) with ground and airborne sensors, and optimize phasing and tasking to maximize coverage and revisit while minimizing resource use<cite id="15">space-based observer placement along libration point orbits</cite><cite id="16">multi-objective Pareto-optimal architecture design and performance analysis</cite>. MILP-based formulations and facility location models (e.g., time-expanded p-Median) enable near-optimal constellation design and sensor-tasking that consider field-of-view and orbital structure, supporting decision-making for CSSA in cislunar space<cite id="1">MILP formulation and TE-p-Median for CSSA constellations</cite>. Capacity-based analyses that include sensor agility (FOV, sweep rate) provide optimized architectures and revisit-rate guarantees for cislunar SDA<cite id="19">capacity and observability analysis with sensor agility</cite>.

## 2. Sensor Platforms and Observing Geometry

Ground-based optical sensors are effective for cislunar tracking when visibility windows align with favorable lunar phases and local times, which strongly influence observability and state uncertainty<cite id="11">visibility-informed covariance analysis and optimal epochs</cite>. Airborne assets (e.g., NASA’s U-2) can extend coverage to cislunar distances and improve detection of small objects, complementing ground networks<cite id="21">U-2 tracking of 10 cm objects at cislunar distances</cite>. Space-based observers in periodic orbits or libration-point orbits can provide continuous coverage during critical events (e.g., lunar eclipses) and transit windows, enhancing short-term tracking continuity<cite id="15">observer placement and tasking for CSSA</cite>.

## 3. Data Fusion and Orbit Determination

Accurate short-term tracking requires fusing optical, radar, and X-band measurements with observability-aware orbit determination. Parametrization approaches using piecewise orbital elements maintain intuitive representations for cislunar trajectories, and uncertainty clouds remain observable for extended periods (e.g., ~80 days) under typical conditions<cite id="12">parameterization and uncertainty propagation for xGEO/cislunar</cite>. Visibility-informed covariance metrics quantify state uncertainty and identify optimal observation windows, guiding sensor scheduling to reduce uncertainty and improve custody maintenance<cite id="11">visibility-informed covariance and favorable windows</cite>.

## 4. Adaptive Sensor Tasking and Observing Strategies

Adaptive tasking strategies tailored to cislunar dynamics improve tracking of multiple targets and non-cooperative objects. Local optimization and modular software frameworks support automated sensor tasking for space-based panchromatic sensors and multi-target association to detect anomalies<cite id="20">adaptive sensor tasking and association for non-cooperative targets</cite>. Reinforcement learning agents can optimally task narrow-field-of-view ground-based optical telescopes in cislunar regimes, outperforming random policies and demonstrating the value of learning-based tasking under complex dynamics<cite id="12">deep reinforcement learning for sensor tasking</cite>.

## 5. Short-Term Tracking and Monitoring Effectiveness

To support short-term tracking and monitoring, optimize phasing and revisit rates using capacity-based analyses and constellation design tools, and schedule observations during favorable lunar phases and local times<cite id="19">capacity-based architecture optimization</cite><cite id="11">optimal observation windows</cite>. Leverage multi-sensor fusion and observability-aware OD to maintain custody and reduce uncertainty over short horizons, and employ adaptive tasking to respond to unexpected maneuvers or non-cooperative behavior<cite id="12">fusion and uncertainty quantification</cite><cite id="20">adaptive tasking for non-cooperative tracking</cite>. Space-based observers can provide continuous coverage during high-dynamic events (e.g., eclipses, transfers), improving short-term tracking continuity and data quality<cite id="15">observer placement and tasking</cite>.

## 6. Practical Recommendations

- Design and operate CSSA constellations using MILP and facility-location formulations to maximize coverage and revisit while accounting for sensor agility and orbital structure<cite id="1">MILP and TE-p-Median formulations</cite>.
- Schedule observations during favorable lunar phases and local times using visibility-informed covariance metrics to reduce state uncertainty and improve custody<cite id="11">visibility-informed covariance analysis</cite>.
- Integrate ground, airborne, and space-based sensors and fuse optical, radar, and X-band data with observability-aware orbit determination<cite id="12">fusion and parametrization</cite>.
- Implement adaptive sensor tasking and learning-based controllers to handle non-cooperative targets and complex dynamics<cite id="20">adaptive tasking</cite><cite id="12">reinforcement learning tasking</cite>.
- Plan for continuous coverage during high-dynamic events with space-based observers in strategic orbits<cite id="15">observer placement and tasking</cite>.

## 7. References

- Cislunar space situational awareness constellation design and facility-location formulations<cite id="1">MILP and TE-p-Median for CSSA</cite>.
- Multi-objective architecture design and performance analysis for cislunar SDA<cite id="16">Pareto-optimal architectures</cite>.
- Capacity-based cislunar SDA architecture optimization with sensor agility<cite id="19">capacity and observability analysis</cite>.
- Visibility-informed covariance analysis for cislunar periodic orbits and optimal observation windows<cite id="11">visibility-informed covariance</cite>.
- Parametrization and uncertainty quantification for xGEO/cislunar trajectories<cite id="12">parameterization and uncertainty clouds</cite>.
- Airborne tracking demonstrations extending to cislunar distances<cite id="21">U-2 tracking at cislunar distances</cite>.
- Adaptive sensor tasking and association for non-cooperative cislunar objects<cite id="20">adaptive tasking framework</cite>.
- Deep reinforcement learning for cislunar sensor tasking<cite id="12">RL-based tasking</cite>.</answer>

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP)-based formulation that simultaneously tackles the constellation design and sensor-tasking subproblems surrounding CSSA. Our approach generates constellation designs that provide coverage with considerations for the field-of-view of observers. We propose a time-expanded p-Median problem (TE-p-MP) which considers the optimal placement of p space-based observers into discretized locations based on orbital slots along libration point orbits, simultaneously with observer pointing directions across discretized time. We further develop a Lagrangian method for the TE-p-MP, where a relaxed problem with an analytical solution is derived, and customized heuristics leveraging the orbital structure of candidate observer locations are devised. The performance of the proposed formulation is demonstrated with several case studies for CSSA constellations monitoring the cislunar Cone of Shame and a periodic time-varying transit window for low-energy transfers located in the Earth-Moon L2 neck region. The proposed problem formulation, along with the Lagrangian method, is demonstrated to enable a fast assessment of near-optimal CSSA constellations, equipping decision-makers with a critical technique for exploring the design trade space.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Yuri Shimane" affiliation="Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30332" /><author name="Kento Tomita" affiliation="Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30332" /><author name="Koki Ho" affiliation="Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30332" /></author_list><url>https://export.arxiv.org/pdf/2408.06238</url><arxiv_url>https://export.arxiv.org/pdf/2408.06238</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2408.06238</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Visibility Informed Covariance Analysis for Cislunar Periodic Orbits</title><summary>Cislunar space domain awareness (SDA) requires maintaining custody of spacecraft, which depends on both visibility and observability. This work develops a visibility-informed covariance analysis framework to evaluate how lunar phase and Earth’s rotation influence the tracking of spacecraft on cislunar periodic orbits. Spacecraft dynamics are modeled using the circular restricted three-body problem, and angle-only optical observations from an equatorial ground station are simulated across a grid of initial observation epochs defined by lunar phase and time-of-day angles. The analysis computes heuristic, covariance-based metrics to quantify state uncertainty and identify favorable observation windows. Results reveal strong dependence of observability on viewing geometry, with optimal epochs aligning with specific lunar phases and local times. These findings provide actionable guidance for mission planning, highlighting how timing and orbit selection can improve state estimation accuracy, ensure flight safety, and enhance SDA capabilities in the Earth-Moon system.</summary><hostname>AMOS Conference</hostname><author_list><author name="Evangelina A. Evans" affiliation="University of Colorado, Boulder" /><author name="Marcus J. Holzinger" affiliation="University of Colorado, Boulder" /><author name="Daniel J. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="cislunar space domain awareness data fusion optical radar X-band tracking Moon L2 libration point orbits visibility observability covariance" search_time="2026年5月19日12时28分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:11"><title>Visibility Informed Covariance Analysis for Cislunar Periodic Orbits</title><summary>Cislunar space domain awareness (SDA) requires maintaining custody of spacecraft, which depends on both visibility and observability. This work develops a visibility-informed covariance analysis framework to evaluate how lunar phase and Earth’s rotation influence the tracking of spacecraft on cislunar periodic orbits. Spacecraft dynamics are modeled using the circular restricted three-body problem, and angle-only optical observations from an equatorial ground station are simulated across a grid of initial observation epochs defined by lunar phase and time-of-day angles. The analysis computes heuristic, covariance-based metrics to quantify state uncertainty and identify favorable observation windows. Results reveal strong dependence of observability on viewing geometry, with optimal epochs aligning with specific lunar phases and local times. These findings provide actionable guidance for mission planning, highlighting how timing and orbit selection can improve state estimation accuracy, ensure flight safety, and enhance SDA capabilities in the Earth-Moon system.</summary><hostname>AMOS Conference</hostname><author_list><author name="Evangelina A. With the Lunar Gateway and increased international efforts to explore and exploit the Moon and cislunar space, a plethora of dynamically complex xGEO orbits are expected to be populated in the coming years. This study addressed topics of fundamental significance for the pressing problem of xGEO SDA: i.e., (1) characterization of the dynamical environment and common scenarios of interest; (2) effective and intuitive parameterizations to describe the orbital motion of xGEO objects in this non-traditional orbital environment; and (3) quantification of uncertainties involved in the orbit determination (OD) process. We then propose a parameterization approach to describe such trajectories based on piecewise orbital elements (geocentric or selenocentric, as the physical picture dictates). We show that, despite the non-Keplerian nature of these restricted three-body orbits, the classical elements are still well defined and provide a time-continuous, intuitive and familiar representation of characteristic xGEO trajectories. Additionally, we model and propagate uncertainties involved in the OD process to better understand the inherent sensitives that plague xGEO and their implications for SDA viewing geometries, required revisit rates, and surveillance volumes. Normality of OD uncertainties is maintained for approximately 40 days, clouds of uncertainty remain fully observable and within the nominal field of view of a ground telescope for approximately 80 days, and close encounters with the Earth and Moon are shown to most significantly affect the size and geometry of propagated clouds of uncertainty.</summary><hostname>AMOS Conference</hostname><publishe

problem: What are the most effective approaches to scaling ion trap quantum computing from small-scale demonstration projects to large-scale systems capable of solving real-world problems? This research should investigate the various proposed scaling strategies, assess their feasibility, and evaluate which approaches are most likely to succeed based on current technological advancements and practical implementation challenges.
final_response:
<answer>## Executive Summary

Trapped-ion quantum computing has demonstrated exceptional gate fidelities and precise control, but scaling to large systems requires addressing engineering and materials challenges. The most promising scaling strategies include planar microfabricated trap arrays, segmented electrode architectures, cryogenic operation, and modular designs. Planar arrays enable dense, reconfigurable 2D connectivity and have shown proof-of-principle operation with adjustable RF electrodes; segmented traps aim to reduce crosstalk and simplify wiring; cryogenics mitigates blackbody radiation and vibration noise; and modularity enables error mitigation and system expansion. While each approach faces practical hurdles—such as uniform electrode fabrication, ion heating, and control complexity—collective progress in microfabrication, cryo-engineering, and control electronics suggests that hybrid, modular systems integrated with error-corrected modules are most likely to succeed in solving real-world problems<cite id="1">review of scaling challenges and outlook for trapped-ion QC</cite><cite id="13">microfabrication challenges and prospects for scalable ion traps</cite><cite id="15">cryogenic trapped-ion clocks and prospects for cryo-computing</cite>.

## Overview of Scaling Strategies

Trapped-ion systems have progressed from few-ion demonstrations to strings of over 100 ions in linear traps, but scaling further demands architectures that enable dense connectivity, uniform control, and robust operation. Reviews emphasize that increasing scale while mitigating decoherence and control errors is the central challenge for near-term applications<cite id="1">review of scaling challenges and outlook for trapped-ion QC</cite>. Several strategies have been proposed to address this, including planar microfabricated trap arrays, segmented electrode traps, cryogenic operation, and modular architectures<cite id="13">microfabrication challenges and prospects for scalable ion traps</cite><cite id="15">cryogenic trapped-ion clocks and prospects for cryo-computing</cite>.

## Planar Microfabricated Trap Arrays

Planar arrays aim to confine ions in a single plane with microfabricated electrodes, enabling dense, reconfigurable connectivity and miniaturization. A planar-electrode ion-trap array demonstrated independent tuning of RF electrodes to vary ion positions and frequencies in two dimensions, supporting large-scale simulations<cite id="7">operation of a planar-electrode ion-trap array with adjustable RF electrodes</cite>. A related design proposed a two-dimensional array of linear traps on a single plane, with segmented electrodes and grounded plates to stabilize ion confinement<cite id="11">planar ion chip design with a 2D array of linear traps</cite>. These arrays are attractive because they reduce the footprint and allow parallel addressing, but they face challenges in achieving uniform electric fields, minimizing ion heating, and integrating thousands of individually controllable traps<cite id="13">scaling challenges for microfabricated ion traps</cite>.

## Segmented Electrode Architectures

Segmented ion traps divide the trap into discrete regions using segmented electrodes, which can reduce crosstalk between ions and simplify wiring compared to fully reconfigurable planar arrays. This design has been explored for scalable quantum information processing, offering a conceptually simple path to microfabrication and large-scale computation<cite id="11">planar ion chip design with segmented electrodes</cite>. Segmented traps can also support localized trapping and Coulomb crystal formation, which may help manage ion motional modes and decoherence in larger systems<cite id="14">segmented ion trap design and operation</cite>. However, achieving uniform trap potentials over large areas and maintaining stable ion confinement at scale remain significant engineering hurdles<cite id="13">microfabrication challenges and prospects for scalable ion traps</cite>.

## Cryogenic Operation

Operating ion traps at cryogenic temperatures can suppress blackbody radiation heating and reduce mechanical vibrations, both of which are major decoherence and heating mechanisms in trapped-ion systems<cite id="15">cryogenic operation reduces blackbody radiation and vibration noise</cite>. Cryogenic trapped-ion clocks have already demonstrated exceptional stability, suggesting that cryo-environments can significantly improve coherence times and ion lifetimes<cite id="15">cryogenic trapped-ion clocks and prospects for cryo-computing</cite>. Integrating cryo-traps with microfabricated electrodes and control electronics is a promising route to scalable, robust systems, but it introduces new challenges in thermal management, materials compatibility, and cryo-compatible electronics<cite id="15">cryogenic operation and engineering challenges</cite>.

## Modular Architectures

Modular designs partition the system into independent ion processor modules that can be linked via entanglement and classical control, enabling error mitigation and system expansion. This approach is attractive because it allows combining multiple modules with error-corrected cores while leveraging the high-fidelity operations already demonstrated in small-scale systems<cite id="1">review of design considerations for future trapped-ion systems</cite>. Modular architectures can also facilitate reconfiguration and upgrades, aligning with near-term applications that require flexible, fault-tolerant operation<cite id="1">near-term applications and system design considerations</cite>. However, achieving deterministic entanglement between modules and maintaining coherence across distributed components remains a key technical challenge<cite id="1">review of scaling challenges and outlook</cite>.

## Materials and Engineering Challenges

Scaling trapped-ion systems hinges on advances in materials and microfabrication to produce uniform, high-aspect-ratio electrodes with precise geometries and low defect densities. Demonstrations of microfabricated trap arrays and segmented designs highlight the need for industrial-grade fabrication processes and rigorous characterization to ensure stable ion confinement and uniform control<cite id="13">microfabrication challenges and prospects for scalable ion traps</cite><cite id="11">planar ion chip design with segmented electrodes</cite>. Cryogenic operation further demands materials that can withstand low temperatures and integration with cryo-compatible electronics, which is an active area of research<cite id="15">cryogenic operation and engineering challenges</cite>.

## Feasibility and Likely Success Pathways

Among the proposed strategies, planar microfabricated trap arrays and segmented electrode traps are the most mature and directly scalable, offering dense connectivity and microfabrication-compatible designs<cite id="7">planar-electrode array operation</cite><cite id="11">planar ion chip design</cite>. Cryogenic operation is a strong enabler that can mitigate heating and decoherence, making it a complementary pathway to improve coherence and stability at scale<cite id="15">cryogenic operation reduces heating and vibration noise</cite>. Modular architectures provide a pragmatic route to error mitigation and system expansion by combining multiple modules with high-fidelity operations<cite id="1">review of design considerations and outlook</cite>.

A hybrid approach that integrates planar or segmented microfabricated traps with cryogenic environments and modular linking is most likely to succeed. This combination addresses the immediate need for dense, reconfigurable connectivity and uniform control while leveraging cryo-environments to extend coherence and stability, and modular linking to manage errors and scale the system<cite id="7">planar-electrode array operation</cite><cite id="11">planar ion chip design</cite><cite id="15">cryogenic operation benefits</cite><cite id="1">modular and system design considerations</cite>.

## Near-Term Applications and Outlook

Trapped-ion systems are well-positioned for near-term applications such as quantum chemistry simulations, optimization, and secure communications, provided scaling challenges are addressed<cite id="1">near-term applications and design considerations</cite>. Continued progress in microfabrication, cryo-engineering, and control electronics, coupled with modular integration, will determine the pace at which large-scale trapped-ion systems can solve real-world problems<cite id="1">review of scaling challenges and outlook</cite><cite id="13">microfabrication challenges and prospects</cite><cite id="15">cryogenic operation and engineering challenges</cite>.</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="ion trap quantum computing scaling architectures 2D arrays microfabricated traps segmented traps surface-electrode traps scalability review" search_time="2026年5月19日12时29分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>Trapped-Ion Quantum Computing: Progress and Challenges</title><summary>Trapped ions are among the most promising systems for practical quantum computing (QC). The basic requirements for universal QC have all been demonstrated with ions and quantum algorithms using few-ion-qubit systems have been implemented. We review the state of the field, covering the basics of how trapped ions are used for QC and their strengths and limitations as qubits. In addition, we discuss what is being done, and what may be required, to increase the scale of trapped ion quantum computers while mitigating decoherence and control errors. Finally, we explore the outlook for trapped-ion QC. In particular, we discuss near-term applications, considerations impacting the design of future systems of trapped ions, and experiments and demonstrations that may further inform these considerations.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Colin D Bruzewicz" /><author name="John Chiaverini" /><author name="Robert Mcconnell" /><author name="Jeremy M Sage" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.04178</url><publish_time>2019年4月9日0时0分</publish_time><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.04178</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>1904.04178</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>2023 Roadmap for Materials for Quantum Technologies</title><summary>Quantum technologies are poised to move the foundational principles of quantum physics to the forefront of applications. This roadmap identifies some of the key challenges and provides insights on materials innovations underlying a range of exciting quantum technology frontiers. Over the past decades, hardware platforms enabling different quantum technologies have reached varying levels of maturity. This has allowed for first proof-of-principle demonstrations of quantum supremacy, for example quantum computers surpassing their classical counterparts, quantum communication with reliable security guaranteed by laws of quantum mechanics, and quantum sensors uniting the advantages of high sensitivity, high spatial resolution, and small footprints. In all cases, however, advancing these technologies to the next level of applications in relevant environments requires further development and innovations in the underlying materials. problem: Research on the price dynamics of chub mackerel in major aquatic markets of Pacific Rim countries, and its interannual variations in weight/length. Combined with oceanographic theory, these research findings can further establish direct correlations between high-quality marine biological resources, aquatic markets, fishery economics, and the marine environment.
final_response:
<answer>## Executive summary

Chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) is a key species in the Pacific Rim fisheries, with major markets in Japan, Korea, and China. Price dynamics in these markets are shaped by supply shocks, processing specifications, and global events, while interannual variations in fish size and weight are linked to climate and overfishing. Combining market price data with biological and oceanographic evidence reveals how marine environmental conditions, fishery practices, and market demand jointly determine the value of high-quality marine biological resources and fishery economics<cite id="2">Pacific mackerel fisheries and price trends</cite><cite id="17">Price data used in stock assessment</cite><cite id="15">Historical decline in body size</cite>.

## Price dynamics in major Pacific Rim markets

In Japan, frozen chub mackerel prices have risen over recent decades due to overfishing and declining landings, with smaller, lower-fat individuals increasingly entering the market<cite id="2">Price increases and overfishing</cite><cite id="5">Smaller, lower-fat mackerel reducing processing yield</cite>. In 2025–2026, the Norwegian–Japan supply chain faced severe price inversion: wholesale prices fell below import costs, pushing downstream processors to substitute cheaper skipjack tuna for mackerel<cite id="4">Price inversion and substitution to skipjack</cite>. In Korea, Norwegian frozen mackerel prices surged in 2025, with 300–500 g规格 averaging 96,000 KRW/kg in July 2025 and climbing to 115,000 KRW/kg by October, while the 10-month average reached 103,000 KRW/kg<cite id="17">July 2025 price</cite><cite id="20">October 2025 price</cite><cite id="16">10-month average</cite>. Korean importers also reported a 124% value increase in January 2025 due to higher prices, underscoring the tight supply and demand<cite id="17">Korea import value growth</cite>.

China’s frozen mackerel exports to ASEAN show pronounced interannual price volatility, driven by trade policy and demand shifts, illustrating how regional market linkages can amplify price swings<cite id="22">China–ASEAN frozen mackerel price volatility</cite>. Domestic Chinese markets for similar species (e.g., horse mackerel) also experienced sharp price spikes in 2025 due to global shortages, with frozen large规格 reaching near 16,800 CNY/t in Dalian<cite id="24">Horse mackerel price spike</cite>.

## Interannual variations in weight and length: biological and oceanographic evidence

Across the northwest Pacific, chub mackerel have exhibited low-age and small-size trends since the 1980s, consistent with increased fishing pressure and environmental variability<cite id="15">Low-age, small size since the 1980s</cite>. In the East China Sea and Yellow Sea, interdecadal analyses of catch and fishery statistics indicate declining resources and shifts in population structure, with length and weight distributions reflecting these changes<cite id="11">Interdecadal changes in resources and population structure</cite>. In the Sea of Japan stock, growth and maturation parameters are tightly linked to ocean conditions, with temperature and productivity shaping recruitment and size at maturity<cite id="12">Sea of Japan growth and maturation tied to environment</cite>.

## Linking markets, economics, and the marine environment

Bioeconomic models show that selective harvesting and market price fluctuations can drive shifts in fishery behavior, with potential negative feedbacks on stock status and economic outcomes<cite id="9">Selective harvesting and price dynamics effects</cite>. For Pacific saury, the introduction of size separators altered landings and prices, contributing to perceived “price collapses” and later removal of the technology, highlighting the need to integrate economic and biological dynamics in policy<cite id="9">Separators and price collapses</cite>. In the Japanese tuna market, exchange rate volatility and supply–demand imbalances have historically driven price fluctuations, reinforcing the sensitivity of seafood markets to macroeconomic and environmental shocks<cite id="19">Tuna market price fluctuations and exchange rates</cite>.

For chub mackerel, the combination of smaller fish entering markets, reduced processing yields, and global supply constraints has directly increased prices and reshaped trade flows and substitution patterns among Pacific Rim countries<cite id="5">Smaller fish and processing yield</cite><cite id="4">Substitution and price inversion</cite><cite id="17">Price trends and import dynamics</cite>. These patterns align with oceanographic theories linking climate variability and overfishing to population dynamics and, consequently, to market value<cite id="15">Climate and overfishing effects</cite><cite id="11">Resource decline and population shifts</cite>.

## Policy and management implications

Monitoring interannual changes in fish size and weight alongside market prices can improve stock assessment and fisheries policy, as biological and economic data together capture the drivers of supply and demand<cite id="17">Price data in stock assessment</cite><cite id="9">Integrated bioeconomic modeling</cite>. Diversifying supply chains and anticipating exchange rate and geopolitical risks (e.g., nuclear discharge impacts) can reduce price inversion and supply shocks<cite id="4">Price inversion and supply chain risks</cite><cite id="19">Exchange rate and supply–demand linkages</cite>. Finally, adaptive management that accounts for climate-driven shifts in growth and maturation will be essential to sustain both biological resources and fishery incomes<cite id="12">Climate effects on growth and maturation</cite><cite id="15">Size trends and climate links</cite>.</answer>
