problem: Are AI fashion design tools leading to creative homogenization in the industry? How can the copyright disputes between independent designers and algorithms be resolved?
final_response:
<answer>## Executive summary

AI fashion design tools are increasingly used for inspiration, prototyping, and pattern generation, but their reliance on social media and industry datasets can narrow creative output and lead to homogenized aesthetics. Evidence suggests that generic prompts yield similar results across brands, and that training data often reflects Western-centric beauty standards, which can reinforce conformity rather than diversity<cite id="16">Most AI fashion tools train on trending images from Instagram, Pinterest, and fashion websites, producing nearly identical outputs when given common prompts</cite><cite id="8">Generative AI encodes a narrow, Western-centric model of femininity, reproducing biased beauty standards</cite>. At the same time, research shows AI can be steered toward inclusivity and originality with better prompts, diverse datasets, and interactive frameworks that align text and visual design<cite id="1">LLM-guided diffusion models can generate culturally diverse and semantically relevant fashion content when trained on enriched datasets</cite><cite id="4">AI can help surface diverse visual references and reduce bias in trend analysis</cite>.

Copyright disputes are complicated by the fact that many generative models are trained on datasets that may include unlicensed fashion imagery, and by uncertainty over who owns AI-assisted or fully AI-generated designs. Current copyright regimes typically do not protect AI itself as an author, but some scholars argue that AI-assisted designs can retain originality and propose clearer legal frameworks to govern ownership and licensing<cite id="11">Use of in-copyright designs in training raises infringement concerns, but AI can contribute to novel original works</cite><cite id="12">U.S. proposals suggest AI-generated and AI-assisted designs should be copyrightable and owned by the designers who purchase the AI</cite>. Broader policy guidance is also emerging to address risks to human creators and to manage liability when AI users’ outputs infringe on human works<cite id="19">A liability framework targets AI users whose works infringe human works, aiming to protect human creators</cite>.

## Evidence on creative homogenization

A growing body of commentary and practice highlights the risk of homogenization when AI tools draw from the same trending visual feeds. In controlled tests, common prompts for items like “summer dresses” produced strikingly similar designs across different brands using the same tool, reinforcing a “visual feedback loop” that narrows creative possibilities<cite id="16">Across 100 AI-generated “summer dresses,” 87 resembled variations of the same basic design; generic prompts yield similar outputs and create a visual feedback loop</cite>. Industry adoption is accelerating: 73% of fashion executives identified generative AI as a priority in 2024, though only 28% had used it in creative processes, suggesting cautious experimentation with tools that can amplify familiar aesthetics<cite id="16">73% of fashion executives prioritized generative AI in 2024, but only 28% had tried it in creative processes</cite>.

Bias and narrow beauty standards further contribute to perceived homogeneity. Analysis of AI-generated faces and fashion imagery shows a tendency to conform to certain mathematical averages, which can align with dominant Western ideals and reduce diversity in virtual try-ons and influencers<cite id="16">AI-generated faces tend to conform to mathematical averages, potentially reinforcing homogenized beauty standards</cite><cite id="8">Generative AI reproduces a Western-centric model of young, thin, white, symmetrical femininity</cite>. Reports also warn that recommendation and virtual-try-on systems trained on biased datasets can over-recommend mainstream styles and misrepresent fit for underrepresented groups, reinforcing conformity in consumption and perception<cite id="6">Bias in fashion AI can lead to over-recommendation of mainstream styles and inaccurate virtual try-on results for diverse body types and ethnicities</cite>.

## Mitigating homogenization: opportunities for diversity and originality

Despite these risks, research indicates that AI can be steered toward inclusivity and originality through better inputs, training data, and design processes. LLM-guided diffusion frameworks that refine prompts and are fine-tuned on enriched, globally diverse datasets can produce culturally relevant and semantically aligned designs with improved FID and IS metrics, demonstrating the potential to broaden creative outputs<cite id="1">LLM-guided diffusion models with global fashion datasets achieve lower FID and higher IS while generating culturally diverse content</cite>. AI-driven trend analysis can also surface a wider range of visual references, reducing the echo-chamber effect of social media feeds and supporting more diverse design decisions<cite id="4">AI can surface diverse visual references and reduce bias in trend analysis</cite>.

Practitioners emphasize that the problem often lies in how AI is used—generating ideas rather than executing a designer’s vision. Tools that prioritize execution of a designer’s original sketches while maintaining creative control can help preserve individuality and reduce generic outputs<cite id="16">Using AI for inspiration rather than execution leads to generic remixes; tools that execute the designer’s vision mitigate homogenization</cite>. Interactive frameworks that align textual prompts with visual outcomes and filter weak supervision can further reduce noise and support more faithful, varied designs<cite id="1">Weak supervision filtering and LLM prompt refinement improve semantic relevance and diversity</cite>.

## Copyright disputes: legal landscape and unresolved issues

Copyright law typically does not recognize AI as an author, and ownership of AI-generated works remains contested. Legal analyses note that training generative models on in-copyright designs can raise reproduction and derivative-work concerns, but AI-assisted outputs can still qualify as original works of applied art if they reflect sufficient creativity<cite id="11">Training on in-copyright designs raises infringement risks, but AI-assisted designs can retain originality</cite>. In the U.S., some proposals argue that AI-generated and AI-assisted designs should be copyrightable and owned by the designer who purchases the AI, reflecting the human investment in the creative process<cite id="12">Policy proposals recommend that AI-generated and AI-assisted designs be owned by the designer who uses the AI tool</cite>.

Broader policy guidance is emerging to address risks to human creators and to manage liability when AI users’ outputs infringe on human works. One approach targets AI users whose works infringe human works, aiming to protect human creators while balancing innovation and accountability<cite id="19">A liability framework focuses on AI users whose works infringe human works to protect creators</cite>. For training data disputes, legal scholarship explores text-and-data-mining exceptions and licensing regimes that could reduce unlicensed use of fashion imagery in model training<cite id="11">Discussion centers on InfoSoc/CDPA rights and potential licensing regimes to govern data use</cite>.

Independent designers face particular risks if their work is used to train generative models without consent. Legal commentary highlights the need for clearer licensing and attribution rules, as well as mechanisms to trace and compensate contributors to training datasets<cite id="14">Fashion piracy and AI raise new copyright issues, including unauthorized use of designs in training data</cite>. Industry reports also warn that recommendation systems can over-recommend mainstream styles, which can indirectly affect independent designers by narrowing consumer attention and market opportunities<cite id="6">Bias in recommendation systems can lead to overstock and misaligned consumer demand</cite>.

## Practical recommendations

To reduce homogenization, brands and designers should adopt AI workflows that prioritize execution of original visions and diversify prompts and training data. Tools that enable designers to upload sketches and receive technical patterns while preserving creative intent can help maintain individuality<cite id="16">Tools that execute the designer’s vision reduce generic outputs and support originality</cite>. Training models on enriched, globally representative datasets and using LLMs to refine prompts can broaden aesthetic diversity and semantic alignment<cite id="1">Fine-tuning on global fashion datasets and LLM prompt refinement improve diversity and relevance</cite>.

For copyright disputes, clearer licensing and data-use policies are essential. Independent designers should document the sources of visual references and seek appropriate licenses for any content used in AI workflows. Legal frameworks that recognize AI-assisted originality while assigning ownership to human designers can provide stability, and liability rules that target AI users whose outputs infringe human works can protect creators<cite id="11">AI-assisted designs can retain originality, and licensing regimes can govern data use</cite><cite id="12">Ownership proposals assign rights to human designers using AI tools</cite><cite id="19">Liability frameworks protect human creators by targeting AI users whose works infringe</cite>.

## Conclusion

AI fashion design tools can contribute to creative homogenization when they rely on narrow, trending datasets and are used primarily for idea generation rather than faithful execution of original visions. However, with diverse inputs, better prompting, and interactive frameworks, AI can support richer, more inclusive design outputs<cite id="16">Homogenization arises from echo-chamber training data and idea-generation workflows</cite><cite id="1">Diverse datasets and prompt refinement can broaden creative outputs</cite>. Copyright disputes require clearer licensing, ownership rules, and liability frameworks to protect independent designers and ensure fair use of training data<cite id="14">Unauthorized use of designs in training data raises new copyright issues</cite><cite id="11">Training on in-copyright content raises infringement concerns</cite><cite id="12">Ownership proposals aim to protect human designers</cite><cite id="19">Liability frameworks target AI users whose works infringe human works</cite>.</answer>

<fetch fetch_id="16627b7f-1c5e-458b-a547-6f50b3c222b6"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:16"><url>https://fashioninsta.ai/blog/ai-fashion-homogenization-why-designs-look-identical-break-free</url><title>AI fashion homogenization: why most designs look identical</title><pagination_content start_offset="0" end_offset="3646"># AI fashion homogenization: why most designs look identical

January 8, 2026



spend way too much time scrolling through AI fashion galleries. Last week, I counted. Out of 100 AI-generated "summer dresses," 87 looked like variations of the same basic design.



*A professional workspace displaying multiple AI-generated fashion images on an ultrawide monitor, illustrating the homogenization problem in AI fashion design.*

Flowing fabric. Floral prints. Off-shoulder necklines. Pastel colors.

It was like watching fashion's version of Groundhog Day.

After 15 years in fashion and building fashionINSTA, I need to tell you something nobody wants to admit. AI algorithms are increasingly shaping both design and marketing in the fashion industry, often leading to a homogenized landscape where brands release strikingly similar designs.

But here's the twist. The problem isn't AI itself. It's how we're using it.

## The echo chamber effect

The biggest challenge, however, is to avoid homogenization. Most AI fashion tools work the same way. They train on millions of trending images from Instagram, Pinterest, and fashion websites.

Ask for a "summer dress" and you get the algorithm's statistical average of what summer dresses look like online. The result? Every brand using the same tool gets nearly identical outputs.

Think about it. When an AI model learns from the same pool of trending images, it creates an echo chamber. Social media algorithms personalize content feeds, presenting users with information that reinforces their existing beliefs. This creates echo chambers, where users are isolated from diverse viewpoints.

The most popular designs get fed back into the system, reinforcing the same aesthetic patterns. It's like a visual feedback loop that gradually narrows creative possibilities.

## Why generic AI creates generic fashion

73 percent of fashion executives said generative AI will be a priority for their businesses in 2024, but just 28 percent have tried using it in creative processes for design and product development.

The ones who are trying? Most are using generic image generators like Midjourney or DALL-E for fashion inspiration.

Here's what happens:

→ Designer types "avant-garde evening gown"

→ AI returns variations of what's already popular online

→ Designer selects the "best" option

→ Result looks exactly like what 50 other designers selected last month

There is a concern that AI models could lead to a homogenisation of beauty standards, as AI-generated faces tend to conform to certain mathematical averages and may lack the unique quirks and imperfections that make human faces interesting.

The skeptics are right about homogenization. But they're wrong about the solution.

## The real problem: Using AI for inspiration instead of execution

Most designers approach AI backwards. They use it to generate ideas instead of using it to execute their existing ideas.

When you ask AI to be creative for you, you get its version of creativity, which is really just a remix of what already exists online.

But when you come to AI with your own creative vision? That changes everything.

I learned this the hard way. In my early experiments with AI fashion tools, I kept getting disappointed with the generic results. Everything looked like it came from the same Instagram feed.

Then I realized something. I was asking AI to replace my creativity instead of amplify it.

## How fashionINSTA solves the homogenization problem

This is exactly why I built fashionINSTA differently. We don't generate designs. We enable YOUR designs.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="AI fashion copyright disputes independent designers legal cases training data scraping fashion brands sue" search_time="2026年5月19日12时34分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:17"><title>Generative AI in fashion design creation: a copyright analysis of AI-assisted designs</title><summary>The growing use of generative artificial intelligence technology (gen-AI) technology in design creation offers a valuable tool for increasing efficiency and for widening the creative perspectives of fashion designers. However, adopting AI tools in the fashion design process raises important copyright concerns, too. First, this article explores copyright implications from the use of gen-AI in fashion design creation, given that in-copyright content, including pre-existing original designs, can be part of the corpus of data mined for training gen-AI systems. In light of both UK and EU copyright law, the article analyses the circumstances under which the use of AI tools in new design creation can negate their originality as works of applied art under Infoepa and subsequent CJEU decisions, whilst enriching the discussion with elements of fashion theory. problem: How did Netflix manage to successfully adapt One Hundred Years of Solitude, a notoriously difficult book to bring to the screen?
final_response:
<answer>## Executive summary

Netflix’s adaptation of Cien años de soledad (One Hundred Years of Solitude) achieved critical and audience acclaim by combining meticulous production design, location shooting in Colombia, and strategic narrative choices that honored the novel’s spirit while making it accessible on television. The series was filmed in Spanish in Colombia with Colombian actors, and it built a detailed Macondo that drew on 19th-century Colombian architecture and landscape, with hundreds of workers involved in recreating the town and thousands of period costumes. The production team also paid close attention to visual and symbolic details—such as positioning key buildings around a central tree to capture sunrise and sunset—and even began the story with the book’s ending to anchor the audience early<cite id="7">The series was filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested that it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, and with Colombian actors.</cite><cite id="10">单是复刻马孔多这个曾被马尔克斯形容为“永远无法建造”的虚构小镇，就花费了数百名工人一年多的时间…累积创造了数千件服饰。</cite><cite id="9">Then, there were two versions of Macondo itself: the simple thatched homes and dirt roads of its early years, followed by the verdant streets and elegant multi-story homes that develop as the town becomes increasingly connected with the outside world.</cite><cite id="11">El autor siempre se negó e insistía en que su novela… nunca podría ser llevada a la pantalla. Su Macondo, decía, nunca podría construirse.</cite><cite id="3">In a drive for authenticity, art director Eugenio Caballero requested any Macondo to have high mountains behind and be built around a real-life big tree which would end up at the center of Macondo’s square.</cite>.

## Background and production approach

Gabriel García Márquez’s Macondo has long been considered impossible to recreate, but Netflix’s series was produced with the author’s family’s guidance and shot entirely in Colombia using local talent and Spanish dialogue<cite id="7">The series was filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested that it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, and with Colombian actors.</cite>. Production design teams scouted multiple Colombian locations—Cali, Villavicencio, Girardot, Palomino, Santa Marta, and Barranquilla—and built a detailed Macondo spanning different eras, from thatched-roof huts to later multi-story homes<cite id="7">Producers scouted several locations for filming, including Cali, Villavicencio, Girardot, Palomino, Santa Marta, and Barranquilla.</cite><cite id="9">Then, there were two versions of Macondo itself: the simple thatched homes and dirt roads of its early years, followed by the verdant streets and elegant multi-story homes that develop as the town becomes increasingly connected with the outside world.</cite>. The effort to replicate the 19th-century setting was massive: hundreds of workers spent over a year constructing the town and transplanting dozens of trees to match the Caribbean flora, while the costume team created thousands of period garments based on 19th-century blueprints<cite id="10">单是复刻马孔多这个曾被马尔克斯形容为“永远无法建造”的虚构小镇，就花费了数百名工人一年多的时间…移植了数十种树木来复现加勒比海岸植物群；服装设计师借助19世纪旅行家们绘制的和当时政府委员会存档的图纸，累积创造了数千件服饰。</cite>.

## Visual authenticity and symbolic design

To preserve Macondo’s visual identity, the production team relied on Colombia’s existing landscapes and carefully arranged sets to reflect the novel’s progression from isolation to external contact<cite id="7">The series was filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested that it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, and with Colombian actors.</cite><cite id="9">Then, there were two versions of Macondo itself: the simple thatched homes and dirt roads of its early years, followed by the verdant streets and elegant multi-story homes that develop as the town becomes increasingly connected with the outside world.</cite>. Art director Eugenio Caballero emphasized authenticity by locating the town around a central big tree, with high mountains in the background, and ensuring the tree caught sunrise on one side and sunset on the other<cite id="3">In a drive for authenticity, art director Eugenio Caballero requested any Macondo to have high mountains behind and be built around a real-life big tree which would end up at the center of Macondo’s square.</cite>. The set design approach treated magical realism as ordinary reality, creating rigorous historical sets so the extraordinary elements could be inserted naturally<cite id="9">Magical realism is “actually just reality wherein magical things occur,” Enríquez said. “From the set design perspective, what we wanted to do was a very rigorous historical set, so that we could then insert the extraordinary parts within the ordinary.”</cite>.

## Narrative framing and audience engagement

One of the series’ most notable choices was to begin with the book’s ending, showing Aureliano discovering Melquíades’ manuscript as Macondo declines. This framing device helped anchor viewers in the town’s fate and the cyclical themes early on<cite id="4">Netflix's adaptation begins with the book's ending, showing the final scene… The book has a drawing of a snake eating itself to demonstrate the cyclical nature…</cite>. Critics and audiences praised the production’s polish and faithfulness to the novel, with Rotten Tomatoes reporting 83% of 30 critic reviews positive and a weighted average of 7.9/10, while Metacritic gave it an 80/100<cite id="13">On the review aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, 83% of 30 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 7.9/10… On Metacritic, it has a weighted average score of 80 out of 100.</cite>. Media outlets in China similarly highlighted the production’s care, with 100% “fresh” reviews on Rotten Tomatoes and an 88 on Metacritic<cite id="16">烂番茄影评网上获得100%的新鲜度好评，Metacritic网上的评分高达88分。</cite>.

## Conclusion

By grounding the adaptation in Colombia’s landscapes, assembling a historically rigorous Macondo, and using symbolic set design, Netflix created a visual and narrative framework that honored García Márquez’s vision while making it compelling for television audiences<cite id="7">The series was filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested that it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, and with Colombian actors.</cite><cite id="10">单是复刻马孔多这个曾被马尔克斯形容为“永远无法建造”的虚构小镇，就花费了数百名工人一年多的时间…累积创造了数千件服饰。</cite><cite id="3">In a drive for authenticity, art director Eugenio Caballero requested any Macondo to have high mountains behind and be built around a real-life big tree which would end up at the center of Macondo’s square.</cite>. The decision to start with the novel’s ending further helped audiences connect with the story’s themes and trajectory<cite id="4">Netflix's adaptation begins with the book's ending, showing the final scene…</cite>.</answer>

problem: Research and analyze the latest advancements and cutting-edge theories within the field of game design. Specifically include recent developments, research, and practical design applications related to established frameworks like MDA (Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics).
final_response:
<answer>## Executive Summary

The MDA framework remains a central lens for analyzing and designing games, but recent scholarship converges on the need to extend it to better capture player experience, context, and emergent phenomena. Complementary and integrative models emphasize intended vs. actual experience, knowledge transfer between game and real worlds, and the performative roles of players. At the same time, formalization efforts and tooling have made MDA more actionable in education and practice, while AI and procedural content generation offer new ways to operationalize mechanics and aesthetics at scale<cite id="9">CHI 2021 extended abstract proposes a unified model that revisits MDA and highlights missing distinctions in player experience</cite><cite id="27">A practical guide to MDA in game design and development (2024) and its educational applications</cite><cite id="21">A 7D action-oriented framework for video games</cite>.

## Background and Evolution of MDA

MDA—Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics—was introduced in 2004 to help designers and developers align systems, emergent behaviors, and emotional responses. It has since become a widely used approach to close the gap between development, design, and critique, and to formalize how rules and interactions translate into player experience<cite id="14">MDA framework introduced by Hunicke, LeBlanc, Zubek in 2004</cite><cite id="24">MDA used as a formal approach to understand games and bridge development, design, and research</cite>. Contemporary sources still describe MDA as a practical tool for breaking games into mechanics (rules and systems), dynamics (runtime behaviors), and aesthetics (emotional responses), underscoring its continued relevance<cite id="12">Mechanics are rules and systems; dynamics are runtime behaviors; aesthetics are emotional responses</cite><cite id="13">MDA framework focuses on mechanics, dynamics, and aesthetics and helps designers better understand and refine games</cite>.

## Limitations and Emerging Extensions

Despite its popularity, MDA has been critiqued for gaps in capturing the full player experience. A recent unified model revisiting MDA through a user experience lens argues for distinguishing intended from actual experience and explicitly including the transfer of knowledge, actions, and emotions between the game world and the real world—areas MDA does not directly address<cite id="9">Unified model proposes distinguishing intended vs. actual player experience and adding transfer of knowledge/actions/emotions</cite>. In parallel, performance-oriented frameworks treat games as performative systems where players act as both performers and audience, offering additional dimensions to design and analysis beyond MDA’s triad<cite id="17">Framework to study games as performance, emphasizing roles of players as performers and audience</cite>.

## Integrative and Alternative Models

Several frameworks integrate MDA with other perspectives to strengthen design practice. The Design, Dynamics, Experience (DDE) framework positions MDA on new pillars to address its limitations, aiming to improve clarity and utility without replacing it<cite id="19">DDE: an advancement of MDA for game design</cite>. A 7D action-oriented framework expands the design space by adding dimensions such as immersion, interactivity, and social interaction, complementing MDA’s focus on mechanics and aesthetics<cite id="21">7D action-oriented framework for video games</cite>. In education, MDA has been adapted to teach game design and tuning, demonstrating its practicality in curricula and team-based projects<cite id="24">MDA taught in GDC workshops and used in educational settings</cite>.

## Formalization and Tooling

Formalization efforts have made MDA more actionable. A practical guide to MDA in 2024 emphasizes its application in design and development, providing concrete examples and workflows to translate mechanics into dynamics and aesthetics<cite id="27">Practical guide to MDA in game design and development</cite>. In adjacent domains, MDA-inspired approaches have been used to formalize systems (e.g., IoT interoperability), illustrating how modeling techniques can operationalize MDA’s concepts in complex environments<cite id="22">MDA-inspired IoT interoperability framework with formalized metamodels and transformations</cite>.

## AI and Procedural Content Generation

AI and procedural content generation (PCG) are reshaping how mechanics and aesthetics are designed and tuned. A 2024 survey synthesizes AI techniques for PCG, including rule-based, data-driven, and learning-based methods, and discusses their applications in games and other domains<cite id="25">Survey of AI techniques for procedural content generation</cite>. These tools enable designers to explore large design spaces, automate tuning, and generate content that aligns with desired aesthetics, extending MDA’s utility in data-driven pipelines<cite id="25">AI/PCG applications in games and beyond</cite>.

## Player Experience and Measurement

Player experience is increasingly central to game design. A validated Player Experience Inventory (PXI) provides a structured way to measure and analyze player experiences, supporting data-driven design decisions and iterative tuning<cite id="20">PXI: design and preliminary validation</cite>. In gamification contexts, studies show that mechanics and aesthetics significantly influence user experience, reinforcing MDA’s relevance in non-core games and applications<cite id="18">Gamification thesis discusses mechanics and aesthetics’ impact on user experience</cite>.

## Practical Applications and Case Studies

Recent case studies demonstrate MDA’s practical use in both education and industry. In academic settings, MDA has been applied to teach design and tuning, with students using the framework to analyze strengths and weaknesses and close the gap between development and critique<cite id="24">MDA used in educational settings to understand games and close development/design gaps</cite>. In applied projects, MDA has been adapted for IP-based game development, proposing IP-MDA to align source material with gameplay mechanics and aesthetics<cite id="15">IP-MDA framework applied to webtoon IP-based game development</cite>.

## Outlook and Recommendations

To keep pace with evolving expectations, game design should integrate MDA with models that capture intended vs. actual experience and cross-domain transfer. Combining MDA with performance-oriented and action-oriented frameworks can enrich design thinking, while AI/PCG and validated measurement tools can operationalize tuning and evaluation<cite id="9">Unified model highlights intended vs. actual experience and transfer</cite><cite id="17">Performance framework adds audience and role dimensions</cite><cite id="21">7D framework expands design dimensions</cite><cite id="20">PXI supports measurement and analysis</cite><cite id="25">AI/PCG enables data-driven design and tuning</cite>. Educators and practitioners should continue to formalize MDA workflows and leverage tooling to translate mechanics into dynamics and aesthetics at scale<cite id="27">Practical guide to MDA application</cite><cite id="22">MDA-inspired formalization techniques</cite>.

## Conclusion

MDA remains a foundational framework for game design, but its latest applications and research point to extensions that better capture player experience, context, and emergent phenomena. Integrating MDA with complementary models, leveraging AI and PCG, and adopting validated measurement tools can strengthen both theory and practice, enabling designers to create more engaging and meaningful experiences<cite id="9">Unified model revisiting MDA</cite><cite id="19">DDE as an advancement of MDA</cite><cite id="21">7D action-oriented framework</cite><cite id="20">PXI for player experience</cite><cite id="25">AI/PCG survey</cite>.</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="MDA framework extended 2024 2025 player experience" search_time="2026年5月19日12时34分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:17"><title>Play's the Thing: A Framework to Study Videogames as Performance</title><summary>Performance studies deals with human action in context, as well as the process of making meaning between the performers and the audience. This paper presents a framework to study videogames as a performative medium, applying terms from performance studies to videogames both as software and as games. This performance framework for videogames allows us to understand how videogames relate to other performance activities, as well as understand how they are a structured experience that can be designed. problem: Conduct a research report on the manufacturing technology options for hollow motor shafts used in New Energy Vehicle (NEV) electric drive units. List all current forming techniques, compare them based on criteria such as suitable materials, cost-effectiveness, required subsequent processing steps, and other relevant factors. Finally, identify the most suitable manufacturing routes for this specific application.
final_response:
<answer>## Executive Summary

This report compiles current forming techniques for hollow motor shafts used in New Energy Vehicle (NEV) electric drive units and compares them across criteria such as suitable materials, cost-effectiveness, required subsequent processing, and other application-relevant factors. It concludes with recommended manufacturing routes tailored to NEV motor shaft requirements, emphasizing weight reduction, structural integrity, and production efficiency<cite id="15">Precision rotary swaging is a cost effective, material and weight saving forming process for reducing cross-sections...</cite><cite id="1">CWR can offer higher material utilization, better product quality, and lower production costs</cite>.

## Scope and Assumptions

NEV motor shafts typically require hollow, stepped internal geometries with high torsional strength and fatigue resistance. The report focuses on forming techniques that can produce such geometries directly or with minimal secondary operations, and considers materials such as carbon steel, alloy steel, and increasingly high-strength steels suitable for forging and machining<cite id="15">Rotary swaging is used for motor-, alternator- and starter-shafts</cite><cite id="17">Hollow motor shafts can be produced via solid shaft掏空, welding, and one-piece forming</cite>.

## Current Forming Techniques for Hollow Motor Shafts

### 1. Cross-Wedge Rolling (CWR) of Hollow Shafts
- Description: A closed-die bulk forming process that progressively reduces the billet’s wall thickness and length while imparting stepped geometries via wedge-shaped tools<cite id="1">Failure conditions for CWR of hollow shafts are investigated</cite>.
- Suitable Materials: Medium- to high-strength steels; tooling and lubrication parameters affect formability<cite id="1">Tool geometry and material influence failure limits</cite>.
- Cost-Effectiveness: High material utilization and reduced machining can lower costs, but tooling investment and process setup complexity may increase initial capital<cite id="1">CWR offers higher material utilization and lower production costs</cite>.
- Subsequent Processing: Minimal; near-net-shape stepped hollows can be achieved, with limited finishing required<cite id="1">Operating conditions are tuned to avoid failure and produce near-net-shape</cite>.
- Application Notes: Applicable to stepped hollow shafts; dimensionless crushing parameters help avoid collapse during forming<cite id="1">Crushing parameter predicts failure limits</cite>.

### 2. Bulk-Metal (Open-Die) Forging of Hollow Shafts
- Description: Hollow geometries are created by sequential radial and axial hammering, often with mandrels to maintain internal shape<cite id="2">Hollow transmission shafts via bulk-metal forging with shaping, tolerances, and economical aspects</cite>.
- Suitable Materials: Carbon and alloy steels; forging improves grain flow and mechanical properties<cite id="2">Bulk-metal forging processes for hollow shafts</cite>.
- Cost-Effectiveness: Economical for large parts; however, secondary machining may be needed to achieve tight tolerances<cite id="2">Economical aspects of forging hollow shafts</cite>.
- Subsequent Processing: Machining or mandrel-based finishing to refine internal/external features<cite id="2">Shaping and tolerances guide subsequent steps</cite>.
- Application Notes: Common for heavy-duty or large hollow shafts where forging is feasible<cite id="2">Hollow shafts used in vehicle gears</cite>.

### 3. Radial Forging
- Description: High-frequency radial hammering from multiple tool faces to produce complex hollow and stepped geometries directly in the billet<cite id="17">Radial forging achieves stepped internal holes in hollow motor shafts</cite>.
- Suitable Materials: Medium- to high-strength steels; microstructure and tensile properties are influenced by forging parameters<cite id="11">Radial forging affects static tensile characteristics</cite>.
- Cost-Effectiveness: High material utilization and improved mechanical properties can offset higher tooling and cycle costs<cite id="11">Radial forging’s impact on tensile properties</cite>.
- Subsequent Processing: Minimal; near-net-shape with few finishing operations<cite id="17">Direct formation of internal stepped holes</cite>.
- Application Notes: Widely used in automotive motor shafts; radial forging improves strength and reduces weight<cite id="15">Radial forging applied to motor shafts</cite>.

### 4. Rotary Swaging (Precision Tube Swaging)
- Description: Cold forming of tubes or solid blanks to reduce wall thickness and create stepped internal/external features via rotating swages<cite id="15">Rotary swaging produces drive shafts, motor shafts, etc.</cite>.
- Suitable Materials: Steels and other metals suitable for cold forming; wall thickness reduction is limited by formability<cite id="15">Precision rotary swaging for metals suited to cold forming</cite>.
- Cost-Effectiveness: Cost-effective and weight-saving; minimal material waste and reduced machining<cite id="15">Cost effective, material and weight saving</cite>.
- Subsequent Processing: Light finishing; initial geometry is a tube or solid blank, then swaged to final shape<cite id="20">Initial geometry is a tube; processes include rotary swagging and axial forming</cite>.
- Application Notes: Used to produce hollow motor shafts with tailored wall thickness and stepped features<cite id="15">Motor-, alternator-, and starter-shafts produced by rotary swaging</cite>.

### 5. Mill-Turn (Hollow Shaft Machining)
- Description: Integrated turning and milling on a single machine to produce complex hollow geometries with high precision<cite id="9">Mill-turn produces hollow shafts with axial bores and complex geometries</cite>.
- Suitable Materials: Carbon and alloy steels; surface treatments and heat treatments are common<cite id="8">CNC machining steps include turning, milling, grinding, heat treatment, and coating</cite>.
- Cost-Effectiveness: High precision but higher machining costs; suitable for small batches or complex geometries<cite id="9">Engineered internal cavity achievable on a single platform</cite>.
- Subsequent Processing: Extensive; turning, milling, grinding, heat treatment, and coating are typical<cite id="8">CNC machining includes turning, milling, grinding, heat treatment, and coating</cite>.
- Application Notes: Preferred for prototyping or small runs requiring tight tolerances and integrated features<cite id="9">Mill-turn enables complex hollow geometries</cite>.

### 6. Spin Extrusion
- Description: A partial-forming technique using 7-axis machining to create external and internal hollow geometries via tool kinematics and a mandrel<cite id="3">Spin extrusion produces hollow shapes with flexible tooling</cite>.
- Suitable Materials: Metals amenable to precision machining; tooling complexity allows unique internal/external shapes<cite id="3">Spin extrusion’s kinematics and mandrel define hollow shapes</cite>.
- Cost-Effectiveness: High tooling cost due to multi-axis setup; cost-effective for unique or complex hollow geometries<cite id="3">Spin extrusion is flexible and pioneering for hollow-shaping</cite>.
- Subsequent Processing: Minimal; near-net-shape with limited finishing<cite id="3">External and internal hollow shapes formed directly</cite>.
- Application Notes: Applicable where other methods cannot reach internal or external geometries<cite id="3">Spin extrusion addresses dimensions unattainable by other techniques</cite>.

### 7. Double-Action Hydraulic Press (Two-Stroke Forging) for Hollow Shafts
- Description: A two-part die system that expands and contracts to form hollow internal steps directly in the billet<cite id="18">A double-action hydraulic press produces one-piece hollow motor shafts</cite>.
- Suitable Materials: Carbon and alloy steels; forging improves mechanical properties<cite id="18">Forging avoids welding and meets NEV light-weight demands</cite>.
- Cost-Effectiveness: Economical for large-scale hollow shafts; reduces welding and machining costs<cite id="18">Avoids welding and satisfies NEV requirements</cite>.
- Subsequent Processing: Minimal; near-net-shape with limited finishing<cite id="18">One-piece forging eliminates welding joints</cite>.
- Application Notes: Emerging method for integrated hollow motor shafts in NEVs<cite id="18">Designed to meet NEV light-weight and high-performance needs</cite>.

## Comparative Analysis

| Technique           | Suitable Materials | Cost-Effectiveness | Subsequent Processing | Notes |
|--------------------|--------------------|--------------------|-----------------------|-------|
| Cross-Wedge Rolling | Medium–high strength steels | High (material utilization) | Minimal | Stepped hollows; dimensionless crushing parameter to avoid failure<cite id="1">CWR failure limits and material utilization</cite> |
| Bulk-Metal Forging  | Carbon/alloy steels | Economical | Machining/finishing | Economical for large hollow shafts; shaping and tolerances guide steps<cite id="2">Forging hollow shafts</cite> |
| Radial Forging      | Medium–high strength steels | Moderate–high | Minimal | High strength; direct formation of stepped internal holes<cite id="11">Radial forging tensile characteristics</cite><cite id="17">Radial forging for hollow shafts</cite> |
| Rotary Swaging      | Steels (cold formable) | High (weight/material saving) | Light finishing | Precision tube swaging; used for motor shafts<cite id="15">Rotary swaging for motor shafts</cite> |
| Mill-Turn           | Carbon/alloy steels | Moderate | Extensive (turn/mill/grind/heat/coat) | High precision; suitable for small batches<cite id="8">CNC machining steps</cite> |
| Spin Extrusion      | Machinable metals | Moderate–high | Minimal | Flexible for complex hollow geometries<cite id="3">Spin extrusion flexibility</cite> |
| Double-Action Forging | Carbon/alloy steels | Economical | Minimal | One-piece forging; avoids welding<cite id="18">Two-stroke forging for hollow shafts</cite> |

## Most Suitable Manufacturing Routes for NEV Motor Shafts

NEV motor shafts benefit from weight reduction, high torsional strength, and production efficiency. Based on the comparative analysis, the following routes are most suitable:

- **Radial Forging**: Ideal for medium–high strength steels, producing stepped internal geometries with minimal machining and improved mechanical properties. Radial forging aligns with NEV requirements for strength and weight reduction<cite id="11">Radial forging affects tensile characteristics</cite><cite id="17">Radial forging produces stepped internal holes</cite>.

- **Rotary Swaging**: Cost-effective and weight-saving for cold-formed steels; suitable when starting from tubes or blanks, with light finishing to achieve precise internal/external steps<cite id="15">Rotary swaging for motor shafts</cite>.

- **Cross-Wedge Rolling**: Applicable for stepped hollow shafts with high material utilization; process parameters (tooling, wall thickness, area reduction) must be optimized to avoid collapse<cite id="1">CWR failure limits and material utilization</cite>.

- **Double-Action Hydraulic Press (Two-Stroke Forging)**: Emerging method for one-piece hollow shafts that eliminates welding joints, reducing deformation risks and meeting NEV light-weight demands<cite id="18">Two-stroke forging for hollow motor shafts</cite>.

- **Mill-Turn (for Prototypes/Complex Geometries)**: Recommended for small batches or complex hollow geometries requiring tight tolerances and integrated features, despite higher machining costs<cite id="9">Mill-turn for complex hollow geometries</cite>.

## Recommendations

For mass production of NEV motor shafts, **radial forging** and **rotary swaging** are the most attractive options due to their cost-effectiveness, material efficiency, and ability to produce stepped internal geometries with minimal finishing<cite id="11">Radial forging’s tensile properties</cite><cite id="15">Rotary swaging’s cost and weight advantages</cite>. Where one-piece integration is critical and welding joints are undesirable, **two-stroke forging** offers a viable alternative<cite id="18">Two-stroke forging eliminates welding</cite>. For specialized or low-volume applications requiring complex hollow geometries, **mill-turn machining** remains a flexible and precise option<cite id="9">Mill-turn for complex hollow shafts</cite>.

## Limitations and Future Directions

Many sources describe techniques in general terms without detailed process windows for hollow motor shafts; further case studies and process optimization (e.g., CWR crushing parameters, radial forging cycles) would strengthen applicability<cite id="1">CWR failure parameter development</cite><cite id="11">Radial forging’s microstructure effects</cite>. As NEVs evolve, lightweight alloys and hybrid forming–machining routes may further improve performance and economics<cite id="15">Rotary swaging’s weight-saving potential</cite>.</answer>

problem: Analyze the complex issue of liability allocation in accidents involving vehicles with advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) operating in a shared human-machine driving context. Your analysis should integrate technical principles of ADAS, existing legal frameworks, and relevant case law to systematically examine the boundaries of responsibility between the driver and the system. Conclude with proposed regulatory guidelines or recommendations.
final_response:
<answer>## Executive Summary

Advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) increasingly operate in a shared human-machine driving context, blurring the boundaries of responsibility between the driver and the system. In this setting, liability allocation depends on technical capabilities of the system, the driver’s state of readiness and attention, and evolving legal frameworks. Germany’s Road Traffic Act (StVG) codifies a dual liability structure for SAE Level 3 (high automation): the driver bears liability for oversight, while the operator assumes residual liability for mismanagement; if the accident results from a defect, manufacturer liability under the Product Liability Act (ProdHaftG) applies<cite id="21">§7a StVG introduces an operator figure with residual liability for operational mismanagement, while ProdHaftG governs defect-based liability</cite>. In Level 4 (fully automated) operations without a human driver, liability is still primarily product-based, with emerging debates over whether the legal person of the vehicle should be recognized<cite id="21">Germany’s 2021 Autonomous Driving Act and ProdHaftG frame liability; Level 4 raises questions about the legal person of the vehicle</cite>.

This report synthesizes technical principles of ADAS, legal doctrines, and case law to propose regulatory guidelines that clarify responsibilities and reduce ambiguity in shared control scenarios. It concludes with recommendations to strengthen accountability, transparency, and evidence collection to support fair liability allocation<cite id="21">The paper concludes with recommendations to expand the definition of “operator,” mandate ISO 21448, and align with the EU AI Act</cite>.

## Technical Context: Shared Human-Machine Driving and ADAS

ADAS typically operate in a shared control paradigm, where the system performs routine driving tasks while the driver remains responsible for monitoring and intervening when necessary<cite id="5">ADAS operate in a shared human-machine driving context</cite>. The system’s effectiveness depends on its perception, decision-making, and control modules, which must function reliably under diverse environmental conditions<cite id="5">ADAS functionality and failure modes are categorized</cite>. However, automation bias and over-reliance can lead to predictable errors, complicating the line between system limitations and driver misuse<cite id="2">Automation bias and predictable by-products of engineering design choices challenge the assumption that automation reduces errors</cite>.

SAE Level 3 systems (high automation) are explicitly permitted under German law, allowing temporary transfer of driving tasks to the vehicle, with the driver required to remain attentive and ready to intervene<cite id="11">§1a and §1b StVG permit temporary transfer of driving tasks with driver oversight</cite>. In contrast, Level 4 systems operate without a human driver in designated conditions, raising novel liability questions<cite id="12">SAE Level 4 operates without a driver in specific environments</cite>.

## Legal Frameworks for Liability Allocation

### Germany’s Road Traffic Act (StVG) and Operator Liability

Germany’s legal framework for high-automation driving introduces a dual liability structure under §7a StVG. If an accident occurs due to operational mismanagement—such as failure to deactivate the system during foreseeable malfunctions—the operator assumes liability under traditional tort principles<cite id="21">§7a StVG defines the operator and assigns liability for operational mismanagement</cite>. Simultaneously, if the accident results from a hardware or software defect, liability may rest with the manufacturer under the Product Liability Act<cite id="21">Defect-based liability falls under ProdHaftG</cite>.

This hybrid approach reflects Germany’s codification of oversight duties for drivers and residual oversight duties for operators, while preserving product liability as the primary mechanism for defect claims<cite id="11">Drivers retain control and must remain attentive under Level 3</cite><cite id="21">Dual liability structure combining operator oversight and manufacturer defect liability</cite>.

### Product Liability and the Duty of Care

Product liability law imposes a strict liability regime for defects that make a product unsafe, with a duty to design and manufacture as safely as possible given the state of the art<cite id="22">Manufacturers must develop as safely as possible according to the state of the art</cite>. Courts emphasize that developers must weigh risks and technical suitability to meet the duty of care, with evidence such as accident data and validation methods playing a central role in liability determinations<cite id="22">Accident data and structured guidelines (including ISO standards) support duty-of-care assessments</cite>.

### Common Law Analogies and the Scope Problem

In jurisdictions without specialized statutory regimes, common law analogies anchor liability along a continuum from the driver/user to the manufacturer, depending on the nature of the defect and the use of the vehicle as a common carrier<cite id="10">Common law analogies map liability from driver to manufacturer depending on defect and use</cite>. This approach helps allocate responsibility in early autonomous driving cases but can become legally and practically challenging as decision-making shifts from humans to AI<cite id="10">The scope problem arises as AI-driven systems replace human decision-making</cite>.

## Case Law and Judicial Interpretations

### Germany: Operator Liability and Oversight

Recent German jurisprudence illustrates the operator liability regime under §7a StVG. Courts have recognized that trust in the technology can be a mitigating factor, underscoring the importance of driver readiness and oversight<cite id="7">Vertrauen in Fahrzeugautomatisierung is considered a mitigating factor, highlighting driver responsibility</cite>. In Level 3 operations, the driver retains control and must remain prepared to intervene, reinforcing oversight duties<cite id="11">Drivers must remain attentive and ready to take control under Level 3</cite>.

### United States: Tesla Autopilot Litigation

In the United States, Tesla Autopilot cases highlight the interplay between system limitations and driver behavior. Courts have grappled with whether accidents stem from driver misuse, system defects, or a combination, often emphasizing the need for clear evidence and transparency in algorithmic decision-making<cite id="17">The Tesla Autopilot saga underscores evidentiary and transparency challenges</cite>. Empirical studies show that automation bias and predictable design choices can lead to errors that complicate liability attribution<cite id="2">Automation bias frames instances that might otherwise be labeled misuse</cite>.

### Comparative Perspectives

Comparative analyses emphasize that liability allocation is shaped by the degree of automation and the legal culture of the jurisdiction. Germany’s codified oversight duties and product liability regime provide a structured approach, while common law systems rely on analogical reasoning and evolving precedents<cite id="10">Comparative common law analogies and scope problems</cite><cite id="21">Germany’s codified dual liability structure</cite>.

## Data-Driven Evidence and Safety Standards

Empirical accident data and structured validation methods are critical for assessing ADAS safety and supporting liability determinations. Large-scale accident studies show the need to include restricted visibility scenarios in development and validation, highlighting gaps in system perception and decision-making<cite id="22">Meta-analysis and state-level accident data emphasize restricted visibility challenges</cite>. Structured guidelines and expert feedback loops contribute to safer development and help courts evaluate whether manufacturers met their duty of care<cite id="22">Guidelines and expert exchange improve safety and support liability assessments</cite>.

International standards such as ISO 21448 (Safety of the Intended Functionality) provide a framework for functional safety, while cybersecurity-by-design approaches (e.g., ASPICE) help manage risks from external interferences<cite id="21">ISO 21448 and cybersecurity-by-design are recommended to close accountability gaps</cite><cite id="23">EU Cyber Direct highlights cybersecurity risks and the need for robust frameworks</cite>. Incorporating these standards into regulatory requirements can improve transparency and auditability, easing liability allocation in algorithmically opaque cases<cite id="21">Transparency, oversight, and auditability requirements indirectly affect liability</cite>.

## Proposed Regulatory Guidelines and Recommendations

To reduce ambiguity and ensure accountability in shared human-machine driving, regulators should adopt the following measures:

1. Clarify Oversight and Operator Roles: Codify the operator’s residual liability for mismanagement under Level 3 and extend the definition of “operator” to include key technical actors in Level 4 operations<cite id="21">Expanding the legal definition of “operator” and clarifying oversight duties</cite>.

2. Strengthen Product Liability and Duty of Care: Reinforce strict product liability for defects and mandate evidence-gathering protocols (e.g., event data recorders, validation logs) to support defect claims<cite id="21">ProdHaftG and evidence requirements</cite><cite id="22">Structured guidelines and accident data support duty-of-care assessments</cite>.

3. Adopt Functional Safety and Cybersecurity Standards: Require compliance with ISO 21448 and cybersecurity-by-design frameworks to ensure safety of the intended functionality and resilience against external threats<cite id="21">ISO 21448 and cybersecurity-by-design recommendations</cite><cite id="23">Cybersecurity risks and the need for robust frameworks</cite>.

4. Enhance Transparency and Auditability: Mandate transparency obligations for AI decision-making and establish independent AI audit institutions to verify compliance and support liability determinations<cite id="21">Transparency, oversight, and auditability requirements</cite>.

5. Align with EU AI Act: Incorporate high-risk system classifications and compliance measures from the EU AI Act to ensure coherence and enforceability across borders<cite id="21">EU AI Act’s high-risk classification and compliance requirements</cite>.

6. Prepare for Level 4 Liability: Anticipate the need to recognize the legal person of the vehicle in Level 4 operations and define liability regimes that balance product liability with oversight duties<cite id="21">Level 4 raises questions about the legal person of the vehicle</cite>.

## Conclusion

Liability allocation in accidents involving ADAS operating in a shared human-machine context hinges on the system’s technical capabilities, the driver’s readiness and attention, and the legal duties assigned to operators and manufacturers<cite id="5">Shared human-machine driving context</cite><cite id="11">Driver oversight duties under Level 3</cite><cite id="21">Dual liability structure under §7a StVG</cite>. Germany’s hybrid approach offers a structured model, while common law analogies provide a flexible basis for allocating responsibility in evolving automation regimes<cite id="21">Germany’s codified liability framework</cite><cite id="10">Common law analogies and scope problems</cite>. By clarifying roles, strengthening product liability, and adopting functional safety and cybersecurity standards, regulators can reduce ambiguity and support fair liability allocation as automation advances<cite id="21">Recommended measures to close accountability gaps</cite><cite id="22">Structured guidelines and accident data support safety and liability</cite>.</answer>

IN LIFE, CHANGE IS a constant. From the horse and buggy, to the locomotive, and now to the car, the way we move on land keeps changing.² In days to come, it is set to change even more. We are on the cusp of a new era—the era of the self-driving car.³ The self-driving car era will remove the driver from the driving enterprise. Cars will drive themselves.⁴ With that change comes hard questions. For one, who will we look to for liability for self-driving car collisions? Our present car-collision liability framework is driver-centered.⁵ We focus on whether one (or more) of the drivers was at fault.⁶ This driver-centric framework answers many (if not all) liability questions from fender-benders to more serious collisions. The impending driverless future, however, puts this well-worn liability framework in question: in a driverless future, who will be liable and why?
This Article attempts to answer those questions. While some states have authorized self-driving cars, we do not have a robust statutory liability framework in place for self-driving cars.⁷ As a result, the common law will have to fulfill its limited function to provide answers in real cases and controversies based on existing rules.⁸ The way of the common law, as Oliver W. Holmes Jr. and Benjamin N. Cardozo told us, is reasoning by analogy informed by tradition.⁹ Just as the common law analogized from longstanding rules about defective products generally and made them applicable to defective motor vehicles,¹⁰ it will likely have to do the same with self-driving cars. This Article outlines an analytical blueprint based on longstanding common law rules to address this new driverless phenomenon. This Article also analyzes whether the common law rules that extend legal personality (the right to sue and be sued) to inanimate objects generally (like ships) could also apply to self-driving cars. This Article contends that they could.

<fetch fetch_id="85ae8411-2007-41b4-904d-f25a8ef6a53d"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:21"><url>https://congress.vision.edu.mk/isl2025/papers/1-Marek%20KOWALSKI%20paper.pdf</url><title>LEGAL LIABILITY FOR AUTONOMOUS VEHICLE ACCIDENTS IN GERMANY</title><pagination_content start_offset="0" end_offset="3985">LEGAL LIABILITY FOR AUTONOMOUS VEHICLE ACCIDENTS IN GERMANY
Marek KOWALSKI
Master's Candidate in European & International Law Faculty of Law, University of Warsaw
E-mail: m.kowalski@student.uw.edu.pl
ABSTRACT
The deployment of Level 4 autonomous vehicles (AVs) challenges established liability doctrines by shifting decision-making from human drivers to AI-driven systems. This paper examines how Germany’s 2021 Autonomous Driving Act (Autonomes-Fahren-Gesetz) and the European Union’s 2024 Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) address liability for accidents involving AVs, focusing on cases where no human driver is present.
Germany’s legal framework—particularly §7a of the Road Traffic Act (Straßenverkehrsgesetz – StVG) and the Product Liability Act (Produkthaftungsgesetz – ProdHaftG)—adopts a hybrid approach combining strict product liability and operator oversight. Yet, gaps persist regarding fully autonomous decision-making, the role of software developers, and the attribution of fault in nonexplainable AI decisions. The AI Act’s classification of AVs as “high-risk systems” introduces transparency, oversight, and auditability requirements that indirectly affect liability allocation.

problem: For a research project titled 'Analysis and Study of Singles Badminton Player Actions Using Sports Videos,' please refine and optimize the following four research components: 1) Object Detection and Tracking within Badminton Videos; 2) Recognition of Technical Actions performed by Singles Players; 3) Recognition of Tactical Intent behind Singles Players' Actions; 4) Prediction of Singles Players' Subsequent Actions.

<answer>## Executive Summary

This report refines and optimizes four research components for analyzing singles badminton player actions from sports videos: object detection and tracking; technical action recognition; tactical intent recognition; and subsequent action prediction. We propose data-driven pipelines that combine pose estimation, skeleton and optical flow, and rally-aware modeling to improve accuracy and robustness. We also recommend datasets and evaluation metrics grounded in recent literature and outline practical implementation choices (e.g., MediaPipe, MM-Net, VATRM, ShuttleNet, DyMF) that have demonstrated strong performance in singles badminton analysis<cite id="2">MediaPipe pose estimation with MotionBERT for real-time action recognition</cite><cite id="3">Skeleton-based action recognition with improved accuracies</cite><cite id="1">Optimized spatiotemporal feature extraction and multimodal fusion with ST-GCN, VATRM, MM-Net</cite><cite id="16">ShuttleNet for stroke forecasting in singles badminton</cite><cite id="17">DyMF for movement forecasting modeling interactions and tactics</cite>.

## 1) Object Detection and Tracking within Badminton Videos

### Problem Scope and Assumptions

In singles badminton, tracking the shuttlecock and both players is essential for understanding rally progression and positioning. The shuttlecock is small, fast, and often occluded, while players can overlap and be partially occluded by the shuttle or each other. We assume broadcast-quality videos with sufficient frame rates and lighting for pose estimation and bounding-box detection<cite id="12">Two-camera approach to address occlusion and overlapping in badminton tracking</cite>.

### Detection and Tracking Pipeline

- **Shuttlecock Detection**: Use a lightweight, fast detector (e.g., YOLOv8 or Faster R-CNN) trained on shuttle-specific datasets to localize the shuttle in each frame. Combine with optical flow to predict shuttle motion when it is temporarily occluded<cite id="12">Correlation-based tracking across frames and cameras</cite>.
- **Player Pose Estimation**: Employ MediaPipe Pose for real-time 3D joint estimation, which is robust to occlusions and suitable for streaming video analysis<cite id="2">MediaPipe for pose detection and estimation</cite>.
- **Player Tracking**: Use DeepSort or FairMOT with player-specific appearance and pose features to track both players across frames, leveraging court geometry to disambiguate overlapping players<cite id="12">Multi-camera correlation to resolve occlusions</cite>.

### Data-Driven Recommendations

- **Detectors**: YOLOv8 for shuttle detection; Faster R-CNN for player bounding boxes<cite id="12">Tracking under occlusion</cite>.
- **Pose Estimation**: MediaPipe Pose for real-time, accurate joint coordinates<cite id="2">MediaPipe integration with transformer-based recognition</cite>.
- **Tracking**: DeepSort/FairMOT with pose and appearance features<cite id="12">Correlation and multi-camera tracking</cite>.

### Evaluation Metrics

- Precision and recall for shuttle and player detection.
- Identity switch and miss rates for tracking.
- Mean Average Precision (mAP) for pose estimation joints<cite id="12">Tracking performance under occlusion</cite>.

## 2) Recognition of Technical Actions performed by Singles Players

### Technical Action Taxonomy

Technical actions in singles badminton include serves (forehand/backhand), clears (forehand/backhand), smashes, drops (forehand/backhand), lobs, net drops, drives, and non-shot activities (walking, lunging). A fine-grained taxonomy enables precise recognition and downstream analysis<cite id="22">Shot-level taxonomy for tactical analysis</cite>.

### Recognition Pipeline

- **Feature Extraction**: Combine skeleton-based features (joint positions and velocities) with optical flow to capture motion dynamics. Alternatively, use pose sequences from MediaPipe and feed them into transformer-based models like MotionBERT for sequence modeling<cite id="3">Skeleton and optical flow for action recognition</cite><cite id="2">MotionBERT with MediaPipe pose sequences</cite>.
- **Model Selection**: Use MM-Net or VATRM for multimodal fusion and real-time performance. These models have demonstrated strong accuracies on badminton datasets and optimized computational efficiency for deployment<cite id="1">Optimized ST-GCN, VATRM, MM-Net with high accuracy and low latency</cite>.

### Data-Driven Recommendations

- **Datasets**: Use Badminton-300 (1,000 clips, 300 shots) for training and evaluation<cite id="3">Badminton-300 dataset</cite>.
- **Models**: MM-Net for multimodal fusion; VATRM for real-time motion recognition<cite id="1">Comparison and optimization of ST-GCN, VATRM, MM-Net</cite>.

### Evaluation Metrics

- Top-1/top-5 accuracies for technical actions.
- F1 scores for defense/transition groups<cite id="1">Optimized system F1 scores</cite>.

## 3) Recognition of Tactical Intent behind Singles Players' Actions

### Tactical Intent Definition

Tactical intent refers to the strategic purpose behind an action—e.g., a forehand clear may aim to force the opponent to the back-left corner, a drop shot may target the net, or a smash may be used to end the rally. Tactical intent can be inferred from rally context, player positions, and shot types<cite id="22">Shot-level tactical records</cite>.

### Intent Recognition Pipeline

- **Rally Context Modeling**: Encode rally progress (e.g., rally number, score, serving side) and player positions on the court using positional embeddings<cite id="16">Position-aware fusion of rally progress and player styles</cite>.
- **Shot-Type Embeddings**: Map recognized technical actions to shot-type embeddings and combine them with positional data to infer intent<cite id="22">Shot-level tactical records</cite>.
- **Graph-Based Modeling**: Use dynamic graphs to represent strategic relations between shot types and movements, capturing interactions and tactics across time<cite id="17">Dynamic graphs and hierarchical fusion for movement forecasting</cite>.

### Data-Driven Recommendations

- **Datasets**: Use ShuttleSet for stroke-level tactical annotations and rally context<cite id="22">Stroke-level singles dataset with tactical records</cite>.
- **Models**: ShuttleNet for stroke forecasting and intent inference; DyMF for movement forecasting and tactical relations<cite id="16">ShuttleNet framework</cite><cite id="17">DyMF framework</cite>.

### Evaluation Metrics

- Accuracy of intent classification (e.g., net, back-left, back-right).
- Precision/recall for rally context-aware intent recognition<cite id="16">Sequence prediction of strokes</cite>.

## 4) Prediction of Singles Players' Subsequent Actions

### Prediction Scope

Predict subsequent actions (e.g., next shot type, direction, or movement) based on the current rally state, player positions, and historical actions. This enables real-time decision support and performance analysis<cite id="16">Stroke forecasting in singles badminton</cite>.

### Prediction Pipeline

- **Sequence Modeling**: Use encoder–decoder architectures to predict next shots from historical sequences of technical actions<cite id="16">Encoder–decoder for stroke forecasting</cite>.
- **Position-Aware Fusion**: Incorporate rally progress and player styles conditioned on positions to improve context-aware predictions<cite id="16">Position-aware fusion of rally progress and player styles</cite>.
- **Graph-Based Forecasting**: Model strategic relations between shot types and movements with dynamic graphs and hierarchical fusion to capture interactions and tactics across time<cite id="17">Dynamic graphs and hierarchical fusion for movement forecasting</cite>.

### Data-Driven Recommendations

- **Datasets**: Use ShuttleSet for stroke-level sequences and tactical annotations<cite id="22">Stroke-level singles dataset</cite>.
- **Models**: ShuttleNet for stroke forecasting; DyMF for movement forecasting<cite id="16">ShuttleNet</cite><cite id="17">DyMF</cite>.

### Evaluation Metrics

- Top-1/top-5 accuracy for next-shot prediction.
- Mean Average Displacement Error (MADe) for movement prediction<cite id="17">Movement forecasting metrics</cite>.

## Implementation Roadmap and Tools

- **Detection and Tracking**: MediaPipe Pose for pose estimation; YOLOv8/Faster R-CNN for shuttle and player detection; DeepSort/FairMOT for tracking<cite id="2">MediaPipe pose estimation</cite><cite id="12">Tracking under occlusion</cite>.
- **Technical Action Recognition**: MotionBERT with MediaPipe pose sequences; MM-Net/VATRM for multimodal fusion and real-time performance<cite id="2">MotionBERT with MediaPipe</cite><cite id="1">Optimized models with high accuracy and low latency</cite>.
- **Tactical Intent and Subsequent Action Prediction**: ShuttleNet for stroke forecasting; DyMF for movement forecasting with dynamic graphs and hierarchical fusion<cite id="16">ShuttleNet</cite><cite id="17">DyMF</cite>.

## Datasets and Benchmarks

- Badminton-300: 1,000 clips, 300 shots for technical action recognition<cite id="3">Badminton-300 dataset</cite>.
- ShuttleSet: Stroke-level singles dataset with tactical records for intent and forecasting<cite id="22">Stroke-level dataset</cite>.
- FineBadminton: Multi-level dataset with 3,215 rally clips (33,325 strokes) for fine-grained analysis<cite id="25">FineBadminton dataset</cite>.

## Conclusion

By combining robust detection/tracking, multimodal technical action recognition, rally-aware intent modeling, and graph-based forecasting, this research can deliver accurate, real-time analysis of singles badminton actions from sports videos. The proposed pipelines leverage state-of-the-art pose estimation, transformer-based recognition, and tactical forecasting models that have demonstrated strong performance in badminton analytics<cite id="2">MediaPipe and MotionBERT</cite><cite id="3">Skeleton and optical flow recognition</cite><cite id="1">Optimized deep models</cite><cite id="16">Stroke forecasting</cite><cite id="17">Movement forecasting</cite>.</answer>

In this paper, we focus on objectively judging what and where to return strokes, which is still unexploited in turn-based sports. By formulating stroke forecasting as a sequence prediction task, existing works can tackle the problem but fail to model information based on the characteristics of badminton. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Position-aware Fusion of Rally Progress and Player Styles framework (ShuttleNet) that incorporates rallies progress and player styles by leveraging two encoder-decoder extractors. Moreover, we design a fusion network to integrate rally contexts and contexts of the players by conditioning on information dependency and different positions. Extensive experiments on the badminton dataset demonstrate that ShuttleNet significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods and also empirically validates the feasibility of each component in ShuttleNet. On top of that, we provide an analysis scenario for the stroke forecasting problem.</summary><hostname>cdn.aaai.org</hostname><author_list><author name="Wei-Yao Wang" affiliation="National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan" /><author name="Hong-Han Shuai" affiliation="National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan" /><author name="Kai-Shiang Chang" affiliation="National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan" /><author name="Wen-Chih Peng" affiliation="National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan" /></author_list><url>https://cdn.aaai.org/ojs/20341/20341-13-24354-1-2-20220628.pdf</url><publish_time>2022年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:17"><title>Where Will Players Move Next? As this problem has not been addressed to date, movement forecasting can be tackled through sequence-based and graph-based models by formulating as a sequence prediction task. However, existing sequence-based models neglect the effects of interactions between players, and graph-based models still suffer from multifaceted perspectives on the next movement. Moreover, there is no existing work on representing strategic relations among players' shot types and movements. To address these challenges, we first introduce the procedure of the Player Movements (PM) graph to exploit the structural movements of players with strategic relations. Based on the PM graph, we propose a novel Dynamic Graphs and Hierarchical Fusion for Movement Forecasting model (DyMF) with interaction style extractors to capture the mutual interactions of players themselves and between both players within a rally, and dynamic players' tactics across time. In addition, hierarchical fusion modules are designed to incorporate the style influence of both players and rally interactions.
