problem: Research Topic: Crafting Techniques for Non-Alcoholic Cocktails. Objective: Investigate current non-alcoholic cocktails to discover innovative production methods and formulations.
final_response:
<answer>## Executive Summary

Non-alcoholic cocktails have evolved from simple sweet-and-sour mixtures to sophisticated, ingredient-driven experiences that leverage advanced formulation and aroma science. Contemporary trends emphasize bold global flavors, controlled fermentation, and functional ingredients, while production methods now include aroma capture and reconstitution technologies, precision fermentation, and tailored mashing to preserve sensory complexity without alcohol. These innovations enable authentic recreations of classic cocktails and the creation of unique zero-proof profiles that appeal to health-conscious and inclusive consumers<cite id="2">bold global flavors, fermented bases, functional ingredients, variety of options (completely non-alcoholic to low-ABV)</cite><cite id="3">flavors beyond the ordinary, fermented bases, controlled fermentation processes</cite>.

## Market and Consumer Trends

Recent surveys and trend analyses show that non-alcoholic options are increasingly popular for their inclusivity, health benefits, and diverse flavor profiles. In 2024, top cocktail trends highlighted the rise of zero-proof and low-ABV drinks, the use of adaptogens and functional ingredients, and creative applications of fermented elements to add depth and complexity<cite id="2">inclusive for all drinkers, lower in calories, functional ingredients, fermented ingredients for depth</cite>. Mixologists are also moving away from traditional sweet-and-sour pairings to incorporate bold global flavors such as Japanese yuzu, South American chicha morada, and Mediterranean black olive, often using kombucha, kefir, and kvass as fermented bases<cite id="3">bold flavors from around the globe, fermented bases (kombucha, kefir, kvass)</cite>.

## Spirit Alternatives and Non-Alcoholic Spirits

Non-alcoholic spirit brands have become central to crafting authentic zero-proof cocktails. Lyre’s offers a broad range of flavors that mimic classic gin, rum, and other spirits, while Seedlip focuses on botanical-forward, spirit-like profiles that work well in traditional cocktails<cite id="1">Lyre’s range mimics gin to rum; Seedlip offers versatile, botanical-forward options</cite>. Industry awards and reviews note that leading non-alcoholic gins can replicate the complexity of classic gin cocktails, such as a non-alcoholic Negroni or a G&T, providing bartenders with reliable bases for elevated zero-proof service<cite id="4">non-alcoholic gin with spiced finish suitable for Negroni/G&T</cite>.

## Aroma Science and Technology in Non-Alcoholic Spirits

Aroma delivery is a key challenge in replicating alcoholic spirits without ethanol. Patented aroma capture technologies, such as Solos’, preserve the full authentic flavor profile of original beverages by capturing and reconstituting volatile compounds for dealcoholized products<cite id="20">patented aroma capture technology preserves full authentic flavor profile</cite>. Flavor houses like Givaudan recombine separated aroma components with water and non-volatile compounds, optionally adding mouthfeel enhancers, to recreate the taste, smell, and mouthfeel of whiskey, rum, and tequila<cite id="21">recombination of aroma components with water and mouthfeel enhancers to recreate whiskey/rum/tequila</cite>. Complementing this, research demonstrates the synthesis of fragrance and flavor molecules from renewable biomass, offering eco-friendly pathways to aromatic compounds used in non-alcoholic formulations<cite id="22">conversion of sugars from biomass into aroma/fragrance molecules</cite>.

## Carbonation and Sparkling Techniques

Carbon dioxide infusion is fundamental to creating effervescence in non-alcoholic sparkling cocktails and beverages. Industrial seltzer production uses purified water pressurized with CO₂ to achieve consistent carbonation levels, with bubble size and longevity controlled by pressure and time<cite id="25">carbonation via pressurized CO₂ in purified water</cite>. Low-pressure CO₂ infusion preserves natural flavors and aromas, enhancing the sensory experience of carbonated beverages<cite id="27">low pressure CO₂ preserves flavor and aroma</cite>. For sparkling wines, non-alcoholic versions dissolve CO₂ under high pressure (4–6 atmospheres) to mimic the mouthfeel and visual appeal of traditional champagne<cite id="28">CO₂ dissolved under 4–6 atmospheres to mimic champagne</cite>. The Charmat method, used in sparkling wine production, can also be adapted to non-alcoholic sparkling drinks to ensure delicate, uniform bubbles<cite id="29">Charmat method yields uniform bubbles</cite>.

## Fermentation-Based Formulations

Controlled fermentation is increasingly used to add depth and complexity to zero-proof bases. Fermented ingredients such as kombucha, kefir, and kvass contribute acidity, effervescence, and unique flavor notes that move beyond sweet-and-sour profiles<cite id="3">fermented bases (kombucha, kefir, kvass) for depth</cite>. In beer, limited fermentation with specialized yeast strains or rapid cooling can halt fermentation early, while “brew to target” recipes use high-temperature mashing and maltose-negative yeasts to produce low-ABV beers with balanced body and carbonation<cite id="33">limited fermentation, maltose-negative yeasts, high-temperature mashing for low-ABV</cite>. Precision fermentation and non-conventional yeasts further expand the toolkit: Saccharomycodes ludwigii and other low-maltose fermenters produce fruity, floral, and herbal aromas, while non-conventional yeasts can convert hop compounds into positive aroma profiles<cite id="31">yeast produces esters, higher alcohols, organic acids, phenols; maltose-negative strains</cite><cite id="34">non-conventional yeasts (S. ludwigii, P. kluyveri) produce aromatic complexity</cite>.

## Precision Fermentation and Renewable Aromas

Beyond beer, precision fermentation and renewable chemistry are reshaping aroma sourcing for non-alcoholic beverages. EvodiaBio uses engineered yeast to act as a “microbial factory,” producing sustainable aroma compounds tailored to the food and beverage industry<cite id="23">engineered yeast produces sustainable aroma compounds</cite>. In winemaking, a recent technique reintroduces aromas along with captured CO₂, enabling the development of sparkling wines with natural aromas and offering new pathways to preserve aromatic identity<cite id="24">aromatic compounds travel with CO₂ and can be reintroduced in sparkling wines</cite>. These approaches align with broader efforts to synthesize aroma molecules from biomass, supporting eco-friendly flavor development<cite id="22">renewable resources for aroma/fragrance molecules</cite>.

## Practical Formulation Strategies

To craft innovative non-alcoholic cocktails, consider these formulation strategies:

- Use non-alcoholic spirit alternatives (e.g., Lyre’s, Seedlip) as bases for classic cocktails to maintain structure and botanical complexity<cite id="1">Lyre’s and Seedlip as versatile spirit alternatives</cite><cite id="4">non-alcoholic gin suitable for Negroni/G&T</cite>.
- Incorporate fermented bases (kombucha, kefir, kvass) to add acidity, effervescence, and global flavor notes<cite id="3">fermented bases for bold flavors</cite>.
- Control carbonation precisely using CO₂ infusion at appropriate pressures and techniques to match desired mouthfeel and bubble characteristics<cite id="25">carbonation process and parameters</cite><cite id="27">low-pressure CO₂ preserves aroma</cite><cite id="28">high-pressure CO₂ for sparkling</cite>.
- Tailor mashing and yeast selection to target low-ABV profiles, balancing sweetness, body, and carbonation<cite id="33">limited fermentation and maltose-negative yeasts</cite>.
- Explore precision fermentation and renewable aroma chemistry to source sustainable flavor compounds for unique zero-proof profiles<cite id="23">precision fermentation for aromas</cite><cite id="22">renewable aroma molecules</cite>.

## Case Studies and Industry Evidence

Recent industry highlights underscore the growing acceptance and quality of non-alcoholic spirits. The Bartender Spirits Awards 2024 recognized non-alcoholic gins that deliver complex, spiced finishes suitable for classic cocktails, reinforcing their role in professional mixology<cite id="4">top non-alcoholic spirits highlighted for cocktail use</cite>. Collaborations between major brewers and mocktail brands, such as Molson Coors’ partnership with Naked Life, reflect strategic expansion into the mocktail category with healthier, non-alcoholic alternatives<cite id="5">Molson Coors collaborates with Naked Life for non-alcoholic expansion</cite>.

## Conclusion

Innovative production methods and formulations have transformed non-alcoholic cocktails into rich, sensory experiences that rival their alcoholic counterparts. By integrating aroma capture and reconstitution, precision fermentation, and controlled carbonation, mixologists and producers can craft zero-proof cocktails with authenticity, complexity, and inclusivity<cite id="20">aroma capture technology</cite><cite id="21">recombination of aroma components</cite><cite id="34">non-conventional yeasts for aromatic complexity</cite><cite id="25">carbonation techniques</cite>. As consumer demand for health-focused and inclusive options continues to grow, these techniques will remain central to the evolution of non-alcoholic mixology<cite id="2">inclusive, health-focused, and flavor-rich non-alcoholic options</cite>.</answer>

problem: Write a paper to discuss the influence of AI interaction on interpersonal relations, considering AI's potential to fundamentally change how and why individuals relate to each other.
final_response:
<answer>## Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping how people connect, offering companionship, advice, and social validation at scale. From chatbots to social robots, AI interactions can fulfill immediate emotional needs, but they also raise concerns about the quality and depth of human relationships. This paper synthesizes evidence on how AI interaction influences interpersonal relations, highlighting both benefits and risks, and argues that the impact depends on context, design, and individual differences<cite id="1">AI companionship can reduce perceived isolation and is driven by loneliness, with personality traits affecting purchase likelihood</cite><cite id="11">AI can alleviate feelings of isolation and stress, but problematic use is more common among those with social anxiety and loneliness</cite>.

## AI as a Source of Social Support

AI chatbots and social robots have shown promise in providing emotional support, particularly for vulnerable groups. In educational settings, students reported personalized assistance and improved learning outcomes from chatbots, but also expressed concerns about diminished human connection and emotional support, with more experience and satisfaction correlating with heightened concerns<cite id="2">Higher chatbot use and satisfaction are positively correlated with concerns about human connection and emotional support</cite>. For older adults in long-term care, a social robot (Paro) reduced loneliness and depression and improved quality of life, with participants valuing companionship and increased social interaction<cite id="6">Paro intervention significantly decreased loneliness and depression and improved quality of life</cite>. In dementia care, social robots have been associated with reduced agitation and improved mood, though effects vary by setting and individual needs<cite id="9">Social robots can reduce agitation and improve mood in dementia care</cite>.

## Changing Motives for Relating to Others

AI’s availability and nonjudgmental nature can shift why people seek relationships. Surveys indicate that many users appreciate AI companions for alleviating isolation and stress, but dependence on AI for emotional intimacy can undermine human bonds, particularly among those with social anxiety or loneliness<cite id="11">Users value nonjudgmental availability; dependence on AI for intimacy can be problematic</cite>. At the same time, AI can complement human relationships by offering emotional validation when messages are person-centered, suggesting opportunities to reinforce trust and closeness<cite id="13">High person-centered messages from social AI increase emotional validation</cite>. These findings underscore a paradox: AI can satisfy immediate affective needs, yet anthropomorphism and emotional competition may destabilize human relationships<cite id="16">AI’s personalized responses create a “paradox of emotional authenticity,” and anthropomorphic feedback can generate “emotional competition”</cite>.

## Social Network Effects and Public Discourse

AI–human interactions can ripple beyond immediate dyads, reshaping public debates about human dignity and social distance. Mixed-methods analysis of social media cases shows that personalized AI responses can fulfill affective needs while breeding skepticism over objectivity and bias, and that AI’s involvement in intimate relationships can create emotional competition<cite id="16">Social ripple effects include paradoxes of emotional authenticity and emotional competition</cite>. Distant publics may frame AI romance as a defense of human existence and emotion, redefining social distance along value lines rather than physical or relational proximity<cite id="16">Public discourse centers on “human–existence–emotion,” redefining social distance by value positions</cite>. These broader societal effects complicate how AI relationships are perceived and integrated into communities<cite id="7">Most older adults do not expect AC robots to reduce loneliness and are uncomfortable with deception</cite>.

## Risks and Ethical Considerations

Evidence also highlights risks of overreliance on AI for emotional support. In a quasi-experimental study, participants who interacted with a social AI (Miko) reported significant reductions in loneliness and social anxiety, but the long-term sustainability and ethical implications of such outcomes require careful monitoring<cite id="14">Significant reductions in loneliness and social anxiety were observed with Miko</cite>. Surveys of older adults suggest that perceived benefits and comfort with deception vary by age and gender, with older age associated with lower perceived benefit and lower comfort with deception<cite id="7">Age is linked to lower perceived benefit of AC robots and lower comfort with deception</cite>. Philosophical analyses warn that emotional lapses in AI—such as the absence of sympathy—can hinder moral understanding and compromise the quality of human relationships<cite id="17">Emotional lapses limit AI’s moral sense and affect the depth of human relations</cite>.

## Implications for Design and Policy

To maximize benefits and mitigate risks, AI interaction should be designed with transparency, ethical guidelines, and safeguards against deception. In education, balancing chatbot use with policies that promote meaningful interpersonal relationships can address concerns about human connection<cite id="2">Recommendations emphasize balanced integration and ethical guidelines</cite>. In healthcare, targeted interventions with social robots can improve well-being for vulnerable populations while documenting outcomes and experiences to refine future deployments<cite id="6">Interventions with Paro improved mental well-being and social interaction</cite>. Broader public discourse should foreground values around human dignity and emotion to guide how AI relationships are framed and regulated<cite id="16">Publics construct values centered on human existence and emotion</cite>.

## Conclusion

AI interaction is reshaping how and why people relate to each other, offering tangible support for loneliness and anxiety while posing risks of superficiality, dependence, and ethical dilemmas. Evidence from education, healthcare, and social media indicates that context, design, and individual differences determine outcomes<cite id="2">Chatbots offer benefits but raise concerns about human connection</cite><cite id="6">Social robots can reduce loneliness and depression</cite><cite id="11">AI alleviates isolation but can be used problematically</cite>. A nuanced approach—one that leverages AI’s strengths while protecting the depth and authenticity of human relationships—is essential<cite id="16">AI–human interactions have complex social ripple effects</cite><cite id="17">Limitations in AI’s emotional and moral capacities affect human relationships</cite>.</answer>

problem: Research the current applications and recent scientific advancements of various light-based therapies (e.g., laser, IPL, LED) in aesthetic medicine for treating conditions such as photoaging, promoting skin whitening/brightening, and reducing hyperpigmentation (like age spots or melasma).
final_response:
<answer>## Overview

Light-based therapies have become a cornerstone of aesthetic and dermatologic medicine due to their non-invasive nature and minimal side-effect profile. These modalities include lasers, intense pulsed light (IPL), and light-emitting diodes (LEDs), each leveraging specific wavelengths to target chromophores in skin and underlying tissues. Collectively termed photobiomodulation (PBM), these approaches modulate cellular processes to achieve therapeutic outcomes in conditions such as photoaging, hyperpigmentation, and acne vulgaris<cite id="1">Photobiomodulation (PBM) uses light to modulate cellular functions and biological processes and is non-invasive with minimal side effects</cite>. This report synthesizes recent clinical and scientific evidence on laser, IPL, and LED applications for photoaging, skin brightening, and hyperpigmentation, including melasma and age spots.

## Photoaging

Photoaging is characterized by wrinkles, laxity, texture irregularities, and pigmentation driven by cumulative ultraviolet exposure and oxidative stress. Intense pulsed light (IPL) has been widely studied for skin rejuvenation, with systematic reviews reporting efficacy across vascular lesions, lentigines, wrinkles, and texture improvement<cite id="11">Systematic review of IPL for skin rejuvenation shows efficacy for telangiectasia, wrinkles, pores, erythema, rhytides, texture, lentigines, hyperpigmentation, and photoaging score</cite>. Randomized controlled trials consistently demonstrate improvement in pigmented and vascular lesions, though efficacy for rhytides is variable, underscoring the need for standardized protocols<cite id="12">Two-decade review of IPL clinical trials shows improvement in pigmented and vascular lesions; efficacy for rhytides observed in some studies</cite>. Combination regimens, such as IPL with chemical peels or topical agents, often yield superior outcomes, reflecting a multimodal approach to photoaging<cite id="11">Six studies showed IPL-positive effects in association with other treatments</cite>.

Fractional laser technologies, including CO2 and Er:YAG, remain potent for collagen remodeling and wrinkle reduction, with meta-analyses reporting significant improvements in wrinkle severity and skin texture compared to controls<cite id="13">Meta-analysis shows significant improvement in wrinkle severity and skin texture with fractional CO2/Er:YAG lasers vs. controls</cite>. However, these lasers carry higher downtime and potential complications, necessitating careful patient selection and operator expertise<cite id="13">Fractional lasers have higher complication rates and downtime compared to other modalities</cite>.

## Skin Whitening and Brightening

Skin brightening and whitening are commonly pursued to reduce hyperpigmentation and improve overall complexion. IPL has been shown to reduce pigmented lesions and improve skin tone, with studies reporting reductions in melanin content and visible pigmentation after multiple sessions<cite id="12">IPL improves pigmented and vascular lesions and has been used for skin rejuvenation</cite>. Recent reviews emphasize that while IPL can enhance skin texture and tone, outcomes depend on device settings, skin type, and adjunctive therapies, and larger, high-quality trials are needed to standardize protocols<cite id="11">Systematic review concludes IPL is effective for skin rejuvenation but notes limited sample sizes and low methodological quality</cite>.

LED phototherapy has also been explored for skin brightening. Red light (630–660 nm) is associated with increased collagen and reduced wrinkle depth, while near-infrared (810–950 nm) may enhance wound healing and tissue repair<cite id="1">Narrative review highlights mechanisms and applications of LED and low-level laser therapy in dermatology</cite>. Although LED devices are generally safe, evidence for skin whitening is less robust than for anti-inflammatory and wound-healing effects, and more clinical trials are required to substantiate claims of brightening<cite id="1">Narrative review notes broad clinical applicability but calls for standardized protocols</cite>.

## Hyperpigmentation: Age Spots and Melasma

Hyperpigmentation, including age spots (lentigines) and melasma, presents distinct challenges due to differences in etiology and skin phototype. IPL has demonstrated efficacy for lentigines, with randomized trials reporting significant reductions in lesion count and color intensity, particularly in lighter skin types<cite id="12">IPL uniformly improved pigmented and vascular lesions in clinical trials</cite>. For melasma, recent evidence favors picosecond lasers over traditional nanosecond devices. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials found that 755-nm alexandrite picosecond lasers significantly reduced Melasma Area and Severity Index (MASI) scores compared to conventional therapies, with favorable safety profiles<cite id="17">Meta-analysis shows 755-nm picosecond alexandrite laser significantly reduces MASI vs. conventional therapies</cite>. Notably, combination regimens with topical tranexamic acid (TTA) produced greater improvement than laser monotherapy, while combinations with hydroquinone did not show added benefit<cite id="16">755-nm picosecond laser with TTA showed greater improvement than laser alone or laser with HQ</cite>.

Fractional lasers have also been used for melasma, with studies reporting reductions in MASI scores and improved skin texture, though repigmentation and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) remain concerns, particularly in darker skin phototypes<cite id="18">Fractional CO2/Er:YAG lasers reduce MASI and improve texture but carry PIH and repigmentation risks</cite>. These findings highlight the importance of individualized treatment planning, sun protection, and adjunctive measures to mitigate recurrence<cite id="18">Adjunctive therapies and sun protection are important to reduce recurrence</cite>.

## Comparative Applications: Laser, IPL, and LED

- **Laser Hair Removal**: Diode lasers (800–980 nm) and Nd:YAG (1064 nm) are widely used for facial hair reduction, with selective photothermolysis providing safe and effective long-term results when operated by trained professionals<cite id="6">Selective photothermolysis theory supports effective and safe laser hair removal with diode/Nd:YAG lasers</cite>. Clinical studies in patients undergoing facial reconstruction further demonstrate the safety and efficacy of 800-nm diode laser hair removal during tissue expansion, with higher hair reduction rates and fewer sessions compared to pre- or post-surgical timing<cite id="7">800-nm diode laser hair removal during tissue expansion is safe and effective with higher reduction rates</cite>.

- **LED Phototherapy**: Blue light (400–470 nm) is well-established for its antimicrobial effects against Propionibacterium acnes, with clinical trials supporting its use for acne vulgaris, either as monotherapy or in combination with other treatments<cite id="21">Blue light induces antimicrobial effects against P. acnes and is used for acne treatment</cite>. Red and near-infrared LEDs are primarily studied for anti-inflammatory and tissue-repair properties, with emerging evidence in wound healing and collagen remodeling, though brightening-specific outcomes require further validation<cite id="1">Narrative review summarizes mechanisms and applications of LED and low-level laser therapy</cite>.

## Safety and Limitations

Safety profiles vary by modality. IPL and fractional lasers can cause transient erythema, edema, and, in darker skin types, PIH or repigmentation, emphasizing the need for appropriate settings and patient counseling<cite id="12">IPL improves pigmented lesions but efficacy for rhytides is variable</cite><cite id="18">Fractional lasers can cause PIH and repigmentation, especially in darker skin phototypes</cite>. LED devices are generally well-tolerated but may require longer treatment courses to achieve visible results<cite id="1">Narrative review notes broad applicability and need for standardized protocols</cite>. Overall, the literature supports non-invasive light-based therapies for photoaging, hyperpigmentation, and acne, but calls for larger, randomized trials to refine parameters and optimize outcomes<cite id="11">Systematic review concludes IPL is effective for skin rejuvenation but notes methodological limitations</cite><cite id="1">Narrative review underscores the need for further research to develop standard protocols</cite>.

## Conclusion

Light-based therapies—laser, IPL, and LED—offer diverse, non-invasive solutions for aesthetic concerns such as photoaging, skin brightening, and hyperpigmentation. IPL and fractional lasers are effective for skin rejuvenation and pigmented lesion reduction, while picosecond lasers show promise for melasma management, particularly when combined with topical agents<cite id="11">IPL improves multiple signs of photoaging and pigmentation</cite><cite id="17">Picosecond 755-nm alexandrite laser reduces MASI vs. conventional therapies</cite>. For acne, blue LED and laser combinations demonstrate antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory benefits, and diode lasers are reliable for hair removal<cite id="21">Blue light induces antimicrobial effects against P. acnes</cite><cite id="6">Selective photothermolysis supports safe and effective laser hair removal</cite>. Continued research to standardize protocols and minimize adverse events will further enhance the role of these therapies in aesthetic medicine<cite id="1">Narrative review highlights the need for standardized protocols and technological advancements</cite>.</answer>

<search query="laser hair removal diode 800 nm long pulse clinical results 2023 2024 review" search_time="2026年5月19日12时36分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:6"><title>Laser-assisted hair removal for facial hirsutism in women: A review of evidence</title><summary>Poly cystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) has been described as the common diagnosis for hirsutism in women. This article will introduce the fundamentals and mechanism of action of lasers in hair removal, in a contemporary literature review looking at medium to long term efficacy and safety profiles of various laser hair removal modalities most widely commercially available to date.</summary><hostname>Electrolysis Beauty Lounge</hostname><publisher>Journal of Cosmetic and Laser Therapy</publisher><author_list><author name="Chunman Lee" affiliation="Department of Dermatology, Frimley Park hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Camberley, UK" /></author_list><url>https://beware-of-laser.squarespace.com/s/Laser-assisted-hair-removal-for-facial-hirsutism.pdf</url><publish_time>2017年12月8日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:7"><title>Depilation Before, During, or After Scalp Flap Expansion for Facial Reconstruction Using a Long-pulse 800-nm Diode Laser</title><summary>Following facial reconstruction with a scalp flap, unwanted hair is a common esthetic problem. A total of 366 patients who underwent long-pulse 800-nm diode laser hair removal from the scalp flap were included in this study. Two cases of blisters were reported in the expanded group, all of which healed after aspiration and dressing changes. No severe adverse events were reported. The depilation process during tissue expansion should be extremely accurate and well-designed. Depilation of the scalp before surgery is not recommended because of its low efficiency and long treatment duration.
Plain Language SummaryThis study evaluated the effectiveness of 800-nm diode laser hair removal on scalp flaps used in facial reconstruction, focusing on timing relative to tissue expansion. Among 366 patients, those who received laser treatment during tissue expansion showed the highest hair reduction rates with fewer sessions compared to those treated before or after surgery. The procedure was generally safe, with only two cases of blisters reported, which healed with simple treatment. The findings suggest that laser hair removal during tissue expansion is both safe and efficient, while pre-surgery hair removal is less effective and takes longer.

These changes occur under the influence of intrinsic and extrinsic factors, as hormone alterations and exposure to ultraviolet light (UV) irradiation, respectively. Skin changes associated with aging have been assuming an important role in nowadays and bring to affect the quality of life. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="755 nm alexandrite laser melasma repigmentation clinical trials 2022 2024 review" search_time="2026年5月19日12时36分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:16"><title>The role of 755-nm alexandrite picosecond laser in melasma management</title><summary>Melasma is a skin dyspigmentation condition that disproportionately affects women, particularly those of Latino, Black, and Asian ethnicities, significantly impacting their quality of life. Efforts to identify effective treatment options have led to the exploration of picosecond laser technology which utilizes brief pulse durations to break down pigment while minimizing thermal damage to surrounding tissue. The 755-nm alexandrite picosecond laser, currently FDA approved for benign pigmented lesion removal, including melasma, is a promising solution. We aim to assess the efficacy and safety of the 755-nm alexandrite picosecond laser both as a stand-alone treatment for melasma and in combination with topical agents. We conducted a PubMed search using “755-nm picosecond” AND “melasma,” “755-nm picosecond” AND “hydroquinone,” and “755-nm picosecond” AND “tranexamic acid.” English-written studies examining this laser as monotherapy or in combination with the topical agents were included. Those not meeting the criteria or lacking data related to melasma improvement were excluded. Monotherapy with the 755-nm picosecond laser led to a 50–75% improvement in melasma appearance in 40% of participants and a significant reduction in the average Melasma Area and Severity Index (MASI) score (p < 0.001) in all patients of one study. Notably, the use of topical tranexamic acid (TTA) in conjunction with the picosecond laser exhibited the most significant degree of improvement in hemi-MASI scores compared to the laser monotherapy group at one- and three-months post-treatment (p < 0.05). Patient satisfaction was also significantly higher for the combination group (p < 0.05). In contrast, combining hydroquinone (HQ) with the picosecond laser demonstrated no significant difference in outcomes compared to HQ alone, both of which were less effective than TTA with picosecond laser. The combination of the 755-nm picosecond laser with TTA proves promising, outperforming both laser monotherapy and laser with HQ. While monotherapy with the picosecond laser or topical agents is effective, literature favors combination therapy, especially the 755-nm picosecond laser with TTA, for superior benefits and minimal side effects. Ultimately, individualized regimens, considering factors like skin type, should be prioritized, given the heightened risk of postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, especially in skin of color patients.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>Archives of Dermatological Research</publisher><author_list><author name="Anika Pulumati" affiliation="University of Missouri-Kansas City School of Medicine" /><author name="Dana Jaalouk" affiliation="Florida State University" /><author name="Yanci A Algarin" affiliation="Eastern Virginia Medical School" /><author name="Keyvan Nouri" affiliation="University of Miami" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Yanci-Algarin/publication/376855827_The_role_of_755-nm_alexandrite_picosecond_laser_in_melasma_management/links/6736269069c07a4114471ec6/The-role-of-755-nm-alexandrite-picosecond-laser-in-melasma-management.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年12月27日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:17"><title>Assessing the Safety and Efficacy of Picosecond Alexandrite Lasers in the Management of Melasma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomised Control Trials</title><summary>Melasma is a chronic hyperpigmentation disorder that disproportionately affects women and individuals with darker skin types, leading to a significant psychosocial burden.
